cases.title: Epigastric Pain & Nausea
cases.patient: Mr Tan Wei Ming, 62M, Bus Driver

validation.notes: Awaiting cardiology sign-off on dissection re-open criteria and door-to-balloon target.

reasoning.history: Crushing epigastric pain radiating to the jaw/arm with diaphoresis in a patient with cardiac risk factors points to myocardial ischaemia; the absence of a tearing/inter-scapular character argues against dissection.
reasoning.exam: Equal bilateral arm BPs make aortic dissection less likely (but do not exclude it); a soft abdomen with no peritonism argues against a surgical abdomen.
reasoning.bi01: 12-lead ECG first — fast, cheap and diagnostic in epigastric/chest pain with cardiac risk factors; order before bloods.
reasoning.bi06: Lipase deferred ahead of the ECG — pancreatitis is plausible, but a normal lipase does not exclude it (Revised Atlanta needs 2 of 3) and ordering it first delays reperfusion.
reasoning.aortic_dissection: Must-not-miss safety net — re-open if the patient becomes unstable.

cases.vignette: Mr Tan Wei Ming is a 62-year-old male bus driver who walks into the Emergency Department supported by his wife, looking pale and sweaty. He tells you he has had a heavy, squeezing discomfort in his upper abdomen for the past 2 hours. He has also been feeling nauseous and vomited once on the way to hospital.

sigNegs.label: Equal bilateral arm BPs → makes Aortic Dissection less likely (does not exclude it)
No peritonism → makes a surgical emergency (peritonitis, perforated viscus) much less likely
Normal lipase/amylase → makes Acute Pancreatitis less likely (Revised Atlanta: 2 of 3 — pain, enzymes >3× ULN, imaging)

keyTeachingPoints: Inferior MI frequently presents as epigastric (upper abdominal) pain rather than chest pain. Referred pain from the inferior-wall myocardium travels via autonomic (vagal) afferents and can be perceived in the epigastrium. Always think of a heart attack when an older patient with risk factors has unexplained upper abdominal discomfort.

The must-not-miss diagnoses for epigastric pain are Myocardial Infarction, Aortic Dissection, Mesenteric Ischaemia, Ruptured Aortic Aneurysm, and Perforated Viscus. All can be rapidly fatal if missed. They must be on your differential before you start investigating.

Checking both arm blood pressures takes 60 seconds and is a quick, useful bedside test when aortic dissection is suspected. A difference of more than 20 mmHg between arms raises concern that the aorta is torn. Equal pressures — as in this case — make dissection less likely but do not rule it out.

Absence of peritonism (no muscle guarding, no rebound tenderness) on abdominal examination reduces the possibility of peritonitis from a ruptured organ. The mild tenderness on deep pressure only is actually a recognised feature of inferior MI.

The 12-lead ECG is the single most important investigation in this case — free, fast, and diagnostic. In any patient over 40 with unexplained upper abdominal symptoms and cardiovascular risk factors, order the ECG immediately.
ST elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with opposite changes in leads I and aVL is the ECG signature of Inferior STEMI. This pattern is about 95% specific for the diagnosis.

Time matters critically in heart attacks. Every 10-minute delay in opening the blocked artery means approximately 1,000 more heart muscle cells die permanently. This is why the ECG must be done before other tests.

findings.text: Squeezing epigastric pain radiating to jaw and left shoulder, with sweating and nausea — classic features of inferior MI
Crescendo pattern: 2 similar episodes in past week, each resolving spontaneously — unstable angina progressing to MI
Loaded cardiovascular risk profile: hypertension, diabetes, 30 pack-year smoking, father died of MI at 58
ECG: ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL — diagnostic of Inferior STEMI
Troponin 10 times above normal, rising significantly at 3 hours — confirms ongoing heart muscle death
No sudden tearing onset, no radiation to the back between the shoulder blades — both features of dissection are absent
Equal blood pressures in both arms (R: 158/96, L: 156/94 — difference only 2 mmHg). Dissection typically causes >20 mmHg difference
All peripheral pulses equal bilaterally — no evidence of blood vessel compression from a dissection
No pulsatile mass felt in the abdomen — a large AAA may be palpable
Haemodynamically stable (blood pressure maintained) — ruptured AAA typically causes circulatory collapse
Equal peripheral pulses — no evidence of iliac artery involvement from an expanding aneurysm
No history of atrial fibrillation, recent heart attack, or severe hardening of arteries — the usual causes of bowel ischaemia
Soft abdomen without peritonism. Mesenteric ischaemia classically causes 'pain out of proportion to the examination', but frank peritonism develops later as bowel dies
Lactate 1.9 mmol/L (borderline normal). Severe mesenteric ischaemia typically causes lactic acidosis with lactate well above 2.0 mmol/L
Soft abdomen with no peritonism (no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness) — a perforated viscus causes peritonitis with marked guarding and a rigid abdomen
Erect chest X-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm — pneumoperitoneum would be expected with a perforated viscus

cases.approachSub: Reference: Nigel Fong, Algorithms in Differential Diagnosis
cases.approachText: A systematic approach to abdominal pain organises causes by mechanism, ensuring you consider dangerous diagnoses that might not initially come to mind:

approachCats.name: Surgical Emergency
approachCats.eg: Appendicitis, perforated ulcer, bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischaemia, ruptured AAA

approachCats.name: Upper GI
approachCats.eg: Peptic ulcer disease, GORD, gastritis, pancreatitis, oesophageal spasm

approachCats.name: Hepatobiliary
approachCats.eg: Cholecystitis, biliary colic, gallstone in bile duct, hepatitis

approachCats.name: Vascular / Referred ← THIS CASE
approachCats.eg: Myocardial infarction, aortic dissection — pain 'referred' from the chest via shared nerve levels T6-T10

approachCats.name: Metabolic / Systemic
approachCats.eg: Diabetic ketoacidosis, adrenal crisis, high calcium, sickle cell crisis

approachCats.name: Genitourinary
approachCats.eg: Kidney stone, kidney infection, ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy

approachCats.name: Functional / Other
approachCats.eg: Irritable bowel, functional pain, nerve root pain from the spine

cases.approachInsight: The VASCULAR/REFERRED category is the most commonly missed in clinical practice. Inferior MI belongs here — it causes epigastric pain not because the stomach is damaged, but because the pain signals from the lower heart wall travel through the same spinal nerves (T6-T10) as signals from the stomach. Using a systematic approach forces you to consider this category even when the symptom looks entirely GI.
cases.expertNarrative: Inferior STEMI presenting as epigastric pain is the most important diagnostic pitfall in emergency medicine. The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the lower (inferior) wall of the left ventricle, the right ventricle, and the heart's natural pacemaker. Blockage explains all the features: epigastric pain (shared T6-T10 nerve supply), sweating and nausea (vagal activation), and slow heart rate (pacemaker ischaemia). Never let the location of pain determine what organ you think about — in any patient over 40 with cardiovascular risk factors and upper abdominal discomfort, obtain an ECG immediately.
cases.sensitivityNote: Inferior MI is poorly sensitive for 'classic' central chest pain — only about 40-50% of inferior MIs present this way. The rest present as epigastric pain, nausea, jaw pain, or arm pain. This means you must use a highly sensitive screening test (ECG) broadly for any patient over 40 with unexplained upper abdominal symptoms.
cases.specificityNote: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal changes in I and aVL is highly SPECIFIC for inferior STEMI (~95%). Once this ECG pattern is seen, the diagnosis is established with high confidence — competing diagnoses do not need further investigation before starting treatment.

history.find: Began 2 hours ago as a vague upper abdominal ache, gradually worsening to 7/10. Heavy and squeezing quality. Gradual onset — no sudden 'tearing' start. He has had two similar but milder episodes over the past week, each lasting 20-30 minutes and going away on their own.
history.exp: The gradual, squeezing onset is typical of myocardial ischaemia. A sudden tearing onset radiating to the back would suggest aortic dissection. The crescendo pattern (episodes getting more frequent and severe over one week) is a red flag for escalating, unstable heart disease — this is the classic story of unstable angina progressing to a heart attack.

history.find: Pain radiates up to his jaw and to his left shoulder. He also notices a heaviness in his left arm. No radiation to the back.
history.exp: Radiation to the jaw and left shoulder is a classic warning sign for a heart attack. It happens because pain signals from the heart travel through the same nerve pathways as signals from the jaw and arm. Inferior MI (affecting the bottom of the heart) characteristically radiates to the jaw. Absence of radiation to the back argues strongly against aortic dissection, which classically radiates between the shoulder blades.

history.lbl: What makes it better or worse?
history.find: No relief from antacids. No relationship to meals. Not worsened by breathing or moving. Not reproduced by pressing on the abdomen. No relief from sitting forward.
history.exp: Failure to improve with antacids argues against acid reflux and gastritis. No worsening with breathing argues against pleurisy, PE, and pericarditis. No positional relief rules against pericarditis (which typically improves leaning forward). Pain not reproduced by pressing on the abdomen argues against musculoskeletal and peritonitic causes.

history.find: Heavy sweating since pain started. Nauseous and vomited once. Mildly short of breath at rest. No palpitations, no fainting, no blood in vomit, no black stools.
history.exp: Heavy sweating and nausea/vomiting are classic features of inferior MI — the blocked right coronary artery activates the vagus nerve, causing this 'vagotonic' picture. Absence of blood in vomit reduces concern for GI bleeding. Mild breathlessness may mean the heart is not pumping as efficiently as usual.

history.find: Two shorter, milder episodes in the past week — each 20-30 minutes long, going away by themselves, not taken to hospital.
history.exp: A crescendo pattern of escalating episodic pain that resolves spontaneously is the clinical signature of unstable angina progressing to a heart attack. Each episode likely represents transient coronary blockage with spontaneous clot dissolution. This is a high-risk pattern requiring urgent action.

history.find: Hypertension for 10 years (on amlodipine). Type 2 diabetes for 8 years (on metformin). No prior heart attacks, no stomach ulcers, no gallstones, no abdominal surgery.
history.exp: Hypertension and diabetes are two of the most important risk factors for heart disease. Having both significantly raises the probability this is a cardiac cause. Absence of prior stomach problems reduces the likelihood of peptic ulcer disease.

history.find: Amlodipine 5mg daily, Metformin 500mg twice daily. No NSAIDs, no blood thinners, no aspirin. No known drug allergies.
history.exp: No NSAIDs significantly reduces NSAID-induced stomach ulcers as a cause. Knowing medications is essential before starting heart attack treatment — metformin must be withheld before the contrast dye used in the emergency heart procedure (PCI), as it can cause a dangerous acid buildup.

history.find: Father had a heart attack at age 58 and died from it. Mother has high blood pressure.
history.exp: A parent who had a heart attack before age 60 is an independent risk factor for heart disease. This is personally significant — this patient may be experiencing the same fatal event his father had at nearly the same age.

history.find: Smokes 20 cigarettes per day for 30 years (30 pack-years). Alcohol: 1-2 units per week. Bus driver. Mostly sedentary. Lives with wife.
history.exp: 30 pack-years of smoking is a major risk factor for heart disease. Low alcohol makes alcoholic pancreatitis and hepatitis less likely. His job as a bus driver is relevant — after a heart attack, he needs cardiological clearance from the transport authority before returning to work.

history.find: Has been getting more breathless than usual when walking for the past 2 months. No swollen ankles, no waking up at night breathless, no prior palpitations or blackouts.
history.exp: Progressive breathlessness on exertion over 2 months suggests slowly worsening heart function or developing angina. Absence of ankle swelling and night breathlessness makes established heart failure less likely, though early failure could be contributing.

history.find: Normal bowel habits. No blood in stool, no black tarry stools. No difficulty swallowing. No significant weight loss recently. No yellowing of skin or eyes.
history.exp: This negative GI review provides important discriminating information — no rectal bleeding makes GI haemorrhage very unlikely, no jaundice makes liver and gallbladder disease less likely. These negatives help deprioritise the GI causes on your differential.

history.find: No cough, no blood in phlegm, no wheeze. No recent immobility or long flights to suggest PE risk factors.
history.exp: Negative respiratory symptoms reduce the probability of pulmonary embolism as the primary cause. Still a reasonable review given the mild breathlessness, but the overall clinical picture points strongly toward a cardiac cause.

history.find: No pain on urination, no blood in urine, no loin-to-groin pain. Normal urine output.
history.exp: Negative urinary review makes kidney stones and kidney infection very unlikely. Ureteric colic typically causes severe cramping loin-to-groin pain — quite distinct from this presentation.

history.find: No recent travel outside Singapore. Born and raised here.
history.exp: Travel history is not relevant for this presentation. It would matter if malaria, typhoid, or dengue were being seriously considered.

history.find: Patient thinks it is 'too much spicy food' or stomach acid. His main worry is missing work tomorrow — he has a bus route to drive. He wants some antacid tablets and to go home quickly.
history.exp: This is an important component of patient-centred care. His belief that it is a stomach problem is extremely common in patients having inferior heart attacks — this is precisely why the condition is so frequently missed in primary care. His concern about work over his health may reflect denial, which is psychologically common in men experiencing heart attacks. Understanding this allows you to communicate the urgency of the situation effectively.

history.find: Not applicable — patient is male.
history.exp: Not applicable in this male patient. This would be essential in a female patient, where ectopic pregnancy and ovarian torsion are must-not-miss diagnoses requiring specific obstetric history.

pe.find: Visibly distressed and anxious. Pale skin. Profusely sweating (diaphoretic). Slightly short of breath at rest. Sitting upright. No yellow skin or eyes. No signs of chronic liver disease.
pe.exp: Pallor and heavy sweating reflect the body's stress response to a cardiac emergency. The combination of a pale, sweating, distressed 62-year-old with cardiovascular risk factors should immediately raise concern for a serious cardiac event. Absence of jaundice makes liver and gallbladder causes less likely.
pe.lookingFor: Pallor, diaphoresis (sweating), distress — autonomic features of MI; jaundice for hepatobiliary cause

pe.lbl: Vital signs — including BOTH arm blood pressures
pe.find: Blood pressure: Right arm 158/96 mmHg, Left arm 156/94 mmHg — EQUAL (difference only 2 mmHg). Heart rate: 56 beats/minute, regular. Breathing rate: 18/min. Oxygen level: 96% on room air. Temperature: 37.1°C. Fully alert.
pe.exp: CRITICAL NEGATIVE: Equal blood pressures in both arms (difference under 10 mmHg) makes aortic dissection very unlikely — dissection typically causes a difference of more than 20 mmHg because it compresses the artery to one arm. The slow heart rate (56 bpm) is characteristic of inferior MI — the right coronary artery also supplies the heart's pacemaker, so blockage slows it down. No fever argues against an infectious cause.
pe.lookingFor: Both arm BPs (difference >20 mmHg → dissection); HR (bradycardia in inferior MI); SpO₂

pe.find: Neck veins not raised. Normal heart sounds, no abnormal sounds or murmurs. No rubbing sound (pericardial rub). All pulses equal in both arms and legs.
pe.exp: Absence of a pericardial rub reduces likelihood of pericarditis. Equal pulses throughout, combined with equal arm BPs, make aortic dissection less likely — but do not exclude it (dissection can occur with no inter-arm BP difference). Normal neck veins suggest the right heart is not under severe strain yet.
pe.lookingFor: JVP elevation; pericardial rub; muffled heart sounds; murmurs suggesting valvular cause; all peripheral pulses

pe.find: Air entry equal both sides. Lungs completely clear — no crackling sounds, no wheeze, no pleural rub.
pe.exp: Clear lungs argue against pneumonia and against fluid in the lungs from heart failure (which would cause crackling sounds at the lung bases). No pleural rub argues against pleurisy and PE.
pe.lookingFor: Pleural rub (pleurisy/PE); basal crackles (pulmonary oedema); unilateral dullness

pe.find: Abdomen soft and not distended. Mild tenderness to deep pressure only in the upper-middle abdomen — no muscle tensing (guarding), no rigidity, no rebound tenderness. Murphy's sign negative (pressing under right rib cage does not cause sudden pain worsening). Liver and spleen not enlarged. Normal bowel sounds. No pulsatile mass.
pe.exp: CRITICAL NEGATIVE: No peritonism (no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness) makes peritonitis from a perforated organ much less likely. Negative Murphy's sign argues strongly against acute cholecystitis. The mild non-specific tenderness on deep pressure is actually a recognised feature of inferior MI — referred pain from the inferior-wall myocardium via autonomic afferents. No pulsatile abdominal mass makes ruptured aortic aneurysm less likely.
pe.lookingFor: Peritonism (guarding, rebound, rigidity) → surgical emergency; Murphy's sign → cholecystitis; pulsatile mass → AAA; bowel sounds

pe.find: All pulses present and equal in both wrists, elbows, groins, behind knees, and at feet. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. No evidence of poor circulation to any limb.
pe.exp: Equal peripheral pulses throughout, combined with equal arm BPs, comprehensively excludes aortic dissection. Good peripheral circulation confirms adequate heart output despite the slow heart rate.
pe.lookingFor: Equal pulses bilaterally (unequal → dissection/AAA); capillary refill time

pe.find: No tender spots on chest wall. No rib deformity. Pressing on the chest wall does not reproduce the patient's pain.
pe.exp: Absence of reproducible chest wall tenderness argues against costochondritis and rib fractures. A useful negative — if pressing on the chest exactly reproduced the pain, a musculoskeletal cause would become more likely.
pe.lookingFor: Reproducible tenderness on pressing chest wall → musculoskeletal; no reproduction → not musculoskeletal

pe.find: Not performed — no bowel symptoms reported.
pe.exp: Rectal examination is a priority if GI bleeding is suspected. In this case with no bowel symptoms and a strongly cardiac picture, this should not be performed before getting an ECG.
pe.lookingFor: Blood on rectal examination → GI bleed (if suspected)

pe.find: Strength, reflexes, and sensation normal in both arms.
pe.exp: Not indicated in this presentation. There are no neurological symptoms. Performing this before completing the cardiovascular examination in a patient with cardiovascular risk factors and epigastric pain reflects poor clinical prioritisation.
pe.lookingFor: Not indicated — no neurological symptoms; perform only if neurological cause suspected

basic.find: ST elevation 2-3mm in leads II, III, and aVF (the 'inferior' leads). Reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL. Normal sinus rhythm at 56 beats/min. No bundle branch block.
basic.exp: DIAGNOSTIC: ST elevation in the inferior leads with reciprocal changes is the hallmark of an Inferior STEMI — the right coronary artery is completely blocked. This single finding triggers the emergency heart procedure (primary PCI) protocol immediately. All GI diagnoses are now effectively excluded. This should have been the FIRST test ordered.

basic.find: Troponin (hs-TnI): 248 ng/L at arrival (normal under 26 ng/L — about 10 times above normal). Repeat at 3 hours: 1,840 ng/L — rising significantly.
basic.exp: Rising troponin confirms heart muscle cells are dying. Troponin is a protein released when heart cells are damaged. The pattern of a rising level (not just a one-off elevation) is what tells us this is an acute, ongoing event. Combined with the ECG, this confirms Inferior STEMI.

basic.find: Haemoglobin 144 g/L (normal). White cells 11.8 (mildly elevated — a non-specific stress response). Platelets 228 (normal).
basic.exp: Mildly elevated white count is a non-specific response to physiological stress, including a heart attack. Normal haemoglobin makes anaemia unlikely. FBC is a useful pre-procedural baseline but does not help diagnose this case.

basic.find: Sodium 138 (normal), Potassium 4.2 (normal), Creatinine 102 µmol/L (slightly reduced kidney function). All acceptable.
basic.exp: Normal potassium is reassuring — low potassium increases the risk of dangerous heart rhythms during a heart attack. Mildly reduced kidney function is important to know before giving contrast dye for the heart procedure. Pre-procedural baseline, not a diagnostic investigation.

basic.find: All liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin, albumin) within normal range.
basic.exp: Normal LFTs make liver and gallbladder disease as the primary cause unlikely. A useful negative for the GI differential, but not the priority investigation.

basic.find: Lipase 36 U/L (normal — pancreatitis typically causes levels 3 times the upper limit of normal or higher). Amylase 74 U/L (normal).
basic.exp: SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE: A normal lipase makes acute pancreatitis much less likely, but does not exclude it on its own. Under the Revised Atlanta criteria, the diagnosis of pancreatitis requires 2 of 3: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase/amylase >3× the upper limit of normal, OR characteristic imaging findings. Here the pain radiates to the jaw and arm (not the back) and the enzymes are normal, so pancreatitis is unlikely. However, ordering this before getting an ECG in someone with cardiovascular risk factors is poor test sequencing.

basic.find: Blood glucose 11.2 mmol/L (elevated). Urine: glucose present (expected in a diabetic), no ketones.
basic.exp: Mildly elevated glucose is expected in a diabetic under stress. Absence of ketones makes diabetic ketoacidosis very unlikely. Pre-procedural baseline, not a diagnostic tool here.

basic.find: Heart size normal. Mediastinum (space in middle of chest) not widened. Lung fields clear. No collapsed lung, no fluid around the lung.
basic.exp: A normal mediastinal width reduces (but does not exclude) aortic dissection — the equal bilateral BPs have already largely excluded this. Clear lungs argue against pneumonia and pulmonary oedema. Chest X-ray does not diagnose heart attacks. Useful baseline but the ECG comes first.

basic.find: Glucose in urine (expected in his diabetes). No blood, no protein, no signs of infection.
basic.exp: Negative urine makes kidney stones and kidney infection very unlikely. Not a diagnostic investigation in this presentation.

basic.find: pH 7.40 (normal). Oxygen level adequate. Lactate 1.9 mmol/L (borderline — acceptable).
basic.exp: Borderline lactate may reflect mildly reduced heart output. No metabolic acidosis. If significantly elevated (above 2.5), it would raise concern for mesenteric ischaemia or cardiogenic shock. Limited diagnostic value here.

basic.find: D-dimer 0.45 mg/L (mildly elevated — non-specific, elevated in many conditions including heart attacks).
basic.exp: D-dimer is only useful for ruling OUT pulmonary embolism when the clinical probability of PE is LOW. This patient's clinical picture does not have low PE probability, and the ECG has already established the diagnosis. A mildly elevated D-dimer is non-specific and very common in heart attacks. Ordering this here reflects unclear reasoning.

basic.find: CRP 14 mg/L (mildly elevated). ESR 22 mm/hr (normal).
basic.exp: Mild CRP elevation is a non-specific response to any tissue damage, including a heart attack. This test does not help distinguish MI from GI causes and was not a priority investigation in this case.

advanced.find: Complete blockage of the mid right coronary artery (RCA) confirmed. Drug-coated stent successfully placed to open the artery. Blood flow restored. Time from arrival to balloon: 72 minutes (within the 90-minute target).
advanced.exp: DEFINITIVE INVESTIGATION AND TREATMENT: The coronary angiogram confirms total right coronary artery (RCA) blockage as the cause of this inferior STEMI. Emergency PCI restores blood flow and saves heart muscle. The RCA supplies the lower heart wall, the right ventricle, and the heart's pacemaker — explaining all features of this presentation. This is why the ECG had to be done first.

advanced.find: The lower (inferior) and side (inferolateral) heart walls are moving poorly. Mild right ventricular involvement. Pumping function approximately 48% (slightly below normal 55%). No fluid around the heart.
advanced.exp: Confirms inferior STEMI — the walls supplied by the blocked right coronary artery are not moving properly. This distinguishes it from viral myocarditis, which causes global (all-over) poor movement. Right ventricular involvement is clinically important: these patients can collapse if given blood pressure-lowering medications like nitrates.

advanced.find: No tear in the aorta found. Normal aortic dimensions.
advanced.exp: NOT APPROPRIATE: Aortic dissection has already been excluded by equal bilateral blood pressures — that check took 60 seconds. Ordering a CT aortogram in a confirmed STEMI patient delays the emergency heart procedure and causes more heart muscle to die. Every minute of delay matters. This represents a critical sequencing error.

advanced.find: No blood clots in the lung arteries.
advanced.exp: NOT APPROPRIATE: This presentation is not consistent with PE — the ECG has established inferior STEMI, and PE typically presents with fast heart rate and sharp chest pain worsened by breathing. Ordering this delays emergency treatment and reflects a failure to use the ECG findings.

advanced.find: No free gas or fluid. No bowel obstruction or appendicitis. Aorta normal diameter.
advanced.exp: NOT APPROPRIATE: The diagnosis of inferior STEMI has been established. CT abdomen exposes the patient to radiation and contrast dye and delays the heart procedure. This reflects anchoring on the 'epigastric' symptom while ignoring the cardiovascular history and ECG findings.

advanced.find: Procedure deferred — not appropriate in this setting.
advanced.exp: COMPLETELY INAPPROPRIATE: A stomach camera is an elective procedure that would never be done in an acute heart attack. Even if a stomach ulcer were being considered, endoscopy would wait until after the heart is stabilised. This reflects anchoring entirely on the epigastric symptom.

advanced.find: No gallstones. Normal liver and bile ducts. Normal kidney. Aorta normal diameter.
advanced.exp: Abdominal ultrasound would be appropriate as a first-line test if gallbladder disease were high on the differential. After the ECG has confirmed inferior STEMI, this scan is not indicated. The normal aortic diameter further supports against a ruptured aneurysm.

advanced.find: Not performed — not clinically indicated.
advanced.exp: NOT APPROPRIATE: A V/Q scan is an alternative way to look for pulmonary embolism, used in patients who cannot have contrast dye. In this case, the ECG has established the diagnosis. Selecting this shows a misunderstanding of both the diagnosis and when this scan is used.

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: Equal bilateral arm BPs (difference <10 mmHg) make aortic dissection less likely — a >20 mmHg difference would raise concern — but equal pressures do not exclude it; the absent tearing/inter-scapular pain is more reassuring
No peritonism, soft abdomen, no pulsatile mass — ruptured AAA presents with haemodynamic instability and peritonism
Soft abdomen without peritonism argues against mesenteric ischaemia — bowel ischaemia classically causes 'pain out of proportion to exam', but frank peritonism develops as bowel dies
Soft abdomen with no peritonism argues against a perforated viscus — perforation causes peritonitis with guarding and rigidity
ECG: ST elevation in II, III, aVF — this RULES IN MI (confirmed diagnosis, should be #1)

cases.title: Progressive Breathlessness & Weight Loss
cases.patient: Mr Lim Ah Kow, 58M, Retired Factory Worker

reasoning.bi01: Chest X-ray is the key first-line test — a central hilar mass reframes the whole presentation toward lung cancer.
reasoning.addisonian_crisis: Exclude adrenal insufficiency (9 am cortisol ± Synacthen) before attributing the hyponatraemia to SIADH — it is reversible and life-threatening.

cases.vignette: Mr Lim Ah Kow, a 58-year-old retired factory worker, is brought into the Emergency Department by his son. His son reports that his father has been getting progressively more breathless over the past 6 weeks, and has lost a lot of weight. Today, he seems more confused and unsteady than usual.
cases.finalDx: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) with Paraneoplastic SIADH

sigNegs.label: No raised JVP, no muffled heart sounds → cardiac tamponade less likely
Euvolaemia confirmed clinically → consistent with SIADH, not dehydration or fluid overload
Normal D-dimer → effectively excludes PE given subacute course and low pre-test probability
Sodium 122 mmol/L (euvolaemic) → confirms SIADH pattern; triggers Addison's/hypothyroid exclusion workup

keyTeachingPoints: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive lung cancer strongly associated with heavy smoking. It arises centrally, near the main airways, and is typically already widespread at diagnosis. It is the lung cancer most strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes.

Paraneoplastic syndromes occur when tumour cells produce substances that affect other organs — without cancer having directly spread there. SCLC is strongly associated with SIADH via ectopic ADH production.

SIADH causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia. The kidneys retain excess water, diluting the blood sodium. When sodium falls below approximately 125 mmol/L, brain swelling causes confusion. The diagnostic criteria for SIADH are: low serum sodium + low serum osmolality + inappropriately concentrated urine + high urine sodium (>40 mmol/L) + euvolaemia + exclusion of adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and diuretics.

In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, always consider Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency) as an important and potentially life-threatening cause, as it can closely mimic SIADH biochemically. A 9 am serum cortisol should be checked early, and a Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test is often used to confirm the diagnosis when appropriate. It is essential to exclude adrenal insufficiency before attributing hyponatraemia to SIADH, as it is immediately treatable with steroid replacement. Particularly, Addisonian crisis should not be missed, and steroid replacement in this condition can be rapidly life-saving.

TB should be considered in patients presenting with chronic cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, and systemic symptoms, particularly in high-risk or endemic settings. In suspected cases, appropriate infection-control precautions and isolation should be initiated early until tuberculosis is confirmed or confidently excluded, to reduce the risk of transmission.

Cardiac tamponade is a must-not-miss in any patient with lung cancer and progressive dyspnoea — lung cancer extends to the pericardium more commonly than any other primary cancer. Beck's triad (raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, hypotension) with pulsus paradoxus identifies it clinically; echocardiogram confirms.

When a patient presents with two seemingly unrelated problems (breathlessness AND confusion), always ask whether one diagnosis can explain both. In SCLC, the cancer explains breathlessness (tumour mass, pleural effusion) AND confusion (paraneoplastic SIADH → hyponatraemia). The hyponatraemia is a clue pointing to the lungs, not the diagnosis itself.

findings.text: No recent immobility, long-haul travel, or leg swelling — classic acute PE risk factors absent
Gradual progressive onset over 6 weeks — acute massive or submassive PE would cause sudden haemodynamic deterioration, not a 6-week subacute course
Normal D-dimer (0.38 mg/L) — in this context (subacute course, no classic risk factors), a normal D-dimer effectively excludes clinically significant PE
Heart rate 96 bpm, SpO2 91% — while consistent with hypoxaemia, haemodynamic compromise from PE (tachycardia >100, hypotension, raised JVP) is not clearly present
JVP not elevated — tamponade causes markedly raised JVP as one of Beck's triad; absent here
Heart sounds normal, not muffled — tamponade causes muffled heart sounds from surrounding fluid
Blood pressure 108/70 mmHg maintained — tamponade causes progressive hypotension and circulatory compromise
Note: tamponade remains possible in cancer patients without classic Beck's triad — echocardiogram would definitively exclude it if clinical concern persists
45 pack-years of smoking and central hilar mass on CXR are more consistent with SCLC than TB, which typically causes upper lobe consolidation/cavitation
CXR: large right hilar mass with pleural effusion — not the typical upper lobe consolidation, cavitation, or military pattern of TB
Sputum cytology: malignant cells (small cell carcinoma morphology), no acid-fast bacilli seen; sputum culture negative for TB at 8 weeks

CT chest: large central endobronchial mass with mediastinal nodes and liver lesions — staging pattern consistent with SCLC, not TB. Note: TB and SCLC can co-exist — sputum AFB and culture remain the definitive exclusion
Blood pressure 108/70 mmHg maintained — Addisonian crisis typically causes profound hypotension and haemodynamic collapse
Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (normal) — Addison's typically causes hyperkalaemia alongside hyponatraemia from mineralocorticoid deficiency; normal potassium makes it less likely but does not exclude it

Morning cortisol adequate; Synacthen test: cortisol rises to >550 nmol/L at 30 minutes — adrenal function confirmed intact. Excluding adrenal insufficiency is essential before attributing hyponatraemia to SIADH

cases.approachSub: Reference: Nigel Fong, Algorithms in Differential Diagnosis
cases.approachText: Shortness of breath arises from conditions affecting the lungs, heart, blood, airways, or the body's ability to use oxygen. A systematic approach ensures dangerous causes are not missed:

approachCats.name: Immediately Life-Threatening
approachCats.eg: Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive PE, flash pulmonary oedema — present acutely, not over weeks

approachCats.name: Lower Respiratory — Parenchymal
approachCats.eg: Pneumonia, COPD, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, TB ← must not miss

approachCats.name: Cardiac
approachCats.eg: Heart failure, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade ← must not miss in malignancy

approachCats.name: Malignancy ← THIS CASE
approachCats.eg: SCLC causing direct mass effect, pleural effusion, AND paraneoplastic SIADH → explains both dyspnoea AND confusion via one diagnosis

approachCats.name: Neuromuscular / Metabolic
approachCats.eg: Severe anaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia causing confusion alongside dyspnoea

cases.approachInsight: This case illustrates the principle of 'one diagnosis explaining two problems.' The SCLC explains both the breathlessness (tumour mass + pleural effusion) AND the confusion (paraneoplastic SIADH → hyponatraemia → cerebral oedema). The confusion is the diagnostic clue — it should prompt the question 'why is this patient confused?' which leads to serum electrolytes, which reveals the hyponatraemia, which triggers the SIADH workup, which points back to the lung. The sodium level is not the diagnosis; it is the pointer.
cases.expertNarrative: SCLC presenting with paraneoplastic SIADH is a classic advanced presentation. The central reasoning: (1) A heavy smoker with 6 weeks of progressive cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, and new confusion has SCLC with paraneoplastic SIADH until proven otherwise. (2) The confusion triggers electrolyte testing, which reveals severe hyponatraemia. (3) Euvolaemia on examination localises this to SIADH (not dehydration, not cardiac or hepatic failure). (4) Addison's and hypothyroidism must be actively excluded before diagnosing SIADH — they are life-threatening and immediately reversible. (5) The CXR confirms a central hilar mass, and bronchoscopy biopsy provides histological diagnosis. (6) Treatment of the underlying SCLC is the primary treatment for the SIADH.
cases.sensitivityNote: SCLC has poor sensitivity for 'classic' respiratory symptoms — it frequently presents with weight loss, hyponatraemia, confusion, or neurological symptoms before obvious breathlessness develops. Paraneoplastic syndromes may precede diagnosis. Any heavy smoker with constitutional symptoms and unexplained confusion warrants urgent chest imaging and electrolyte testing.
cases.specificityNote: Tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy or CT-guided) with SCLC histology (small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, neuroendocrine immunohistochemistry — TTF-1, synaptophysin, CD56 positive) combined with a central lung mass on CT is highly specific. SIADH diagnosis requires: hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine + urine sodium >40 mmol/L + euvolaemia + exclusion of Addison's, hypothyroidism, and diuretic use.

history.find: Progressive breathlessness over 6 weeks. Initially only on climbing stairs; now present on walking 50 metres and at rest. No sudden onset. No wheeze. Not worse lying flat. Son confirms it has been worsening gradually week by week.
history.exp: Progressive onset over 6 weeks argues against an acute life-threatening emergency as the primary cause — tension pneumothorax and massive PE present suddenly over minutes. The subacute course over weeks raises concern for a growing structural cause: tumour, pleural effusion, or progressive heart failure. Absence of orthopnoea (worse lying flat) makes heart failure a less likely primary driver.

history.find: Persistent dry cough for approximately 3 months. Over the past 3 weeks, occasionally coughing up small amounts of blood-streaked phlegm (haemoptysis). No foul-smelling purulent phlegm.
history.exp: Haemoptysis in a heavy smoker is a red flag for lung cancer until proven otherwise, but TB must also be seriously considered — both cause haemoptysis in the context of a 6-week progressive respiratory illness. The 3-month duration argues against acute pneumonia. Absence of purulent phlegm makes bacterial pneumonia a less likely primary diagnosis. The triad of progressive dyspnoea + haemoptysis + weight loss in a smoker demands urgent chest imaging.

history.find: Significant unintentional weight loss — son estimates approximately 8–10 kg over 3 months. Very poor appetite for the same period. Low-grade fevers on and off. Night sweats.
history.exp: Significant unintentional weight loss (>5% body weight over 3 months) with anorexia, night sweats, and low-grade fevers constitutes a classic 'B-symptom' pattern raising concern for malignancy or chronic infection. Studies show that weight loss of >5% with breathlessness in this age group carries a 3–4% risk of cancer diagnosis within 6 months, with lung cancer being the most common in a smoker. Pulmonary TB presents with identical constitutional symptoms — both diagnoses must be actively pursued.

history.find: Son reports father has been 'not himself' for about 2 weeks — increasingly confused, forgetful, and unsteady on his feet. No fever. No headache. No limb weakness. No history of dementia. Son says he is 'not himself at all'.
history.exp: New-onset confusion in a patient with probable malignancy should immediately trigger a search for metabolic causes: hyponatraemia (SIADH from lung cancer), hypercalcaemia (from bone metastases), and hypoxaemia. It also raises concern for CNS metastases (common in SCLC) and infectious causes. The gradual onset over 2 weeks without fever or focal deficits favours a metabolic cause over acute infection or vascular event. This is the clinical clue that should prompt ordering serum electrolytes urgently.

history.find: Smokes 30 cigarettes per day for 30 years (45 pack-years — very heavy smoker). Retired 3 years ago from factory work involving assembly of insulation panels (possible asbestos exposure over 15 years). Drinks minimal alcohol (1–2 units per week).
history.exp: 45 pack-years of smoking is the single strongest risk factor for lung cancer, particularly SCLC (which arises centrally near the main airways) and squamous cell carcinoma. Possible occupational asbestos exposure adds risk for mesothelioma and non-SCLC lung cancers. Low alcohol intake makes alcoholic liver disease and its associated dilutional hyponatraemia less likely. In the context of possible TB, it is also worth noting that he does not have clear TB risk factors such as recent travel to endemic areas, immunosuppression, or known TB contacts — though occupational exposure in a factory setting cannot be fully excluded.

history.find: No prior lung conditions. No prior cancer. No known heart disease. No prior adrenal or thyroid problems. No diabetes. No HIV or immunosuppression. No recent TB contacts known.
history.exp: Absence of prior lung conditions means a new diagnosis is needed. No known adrenal disease reduces (but does not exclude) Addisonian crisis as a cause of the hyponatraemia — adrenal insufficiency must still be actively excluded with a Synacthen test, as it is immediately life-threatening and reversible. No hypothyroidism — hypothyroidism is another cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia requiring exclusion. No immunosuppression reduces the likelihood of PCP or atypical opportunistic infection.

history.find: No regular medications. No recent new prescriptions. Specifically: no diuretics (thiazides, loop), no SSRIs, no anticonvulsants, no opiates, no NSAIDs. No known drug allergies.
history.exp: This is a critical exclusion for the SIADH diagnosis: many common drugs cause SIADH and hyponatraemia — especially thiazide diuretics (most common cause of SIADH in the community), SSRIs, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine), and certain chemotherapy agents (cyclophosphamide, vincristine). Absence of all these drugs removes medications as the cause of the hyponatraemia and shifts probability toward a pathological cause. This exclusion is one of the formal diagnostic criteria for SIADH.

history.find: No chest pain. No palpitations. No ankle swelling. No waking up breathless at night (PND). No orthopnoea. No prior heart attacks or known heart disease.
history.exp: Absence of orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND), and ankle oedema makes heart failure a less likely primary cause of breathlessness, though heart failure can coexist with malignancy. No chest pain argues against pericarditis and pleurisy as primary causes. These cardiovascular negatives help shift the differential toward respiratory and malignant causes.

history.find: No recent immobility or prolonged bed rest. No recent long-haul travel. No leg swelling or calf pain. No prior DVT or PE.
history.exp: Absence of classic acute PE risk factors (immobility, recent surgery, recent long travel) significantly reduces PE probability in the acute setting. However, occult malignancy is itself a major chronic prothrombotic risk factor — cancer increases VTE risk 4–7 times. Chronic or recurrent submassive PE could contribute to 6 weeks of progressive dyspnoea even without acute symptoms. D-dimer and clinical probability assessment remain worthwhile.

history.find: No known TB contacts. No recent travel to TB-endemic regions. No prior TB diagnosis or treatment. No HIV or other immunosuppression. Has lived in Singapore throughout adulthood.
history.exp: This is a targeted history to risk-stratify TB. Absence of known TB contacts and recent travel to high-prevalence regions reduces TB probability somewhat. However, TB remains common in Singapore among older adults and cannot be excluded on history alone — particularly given the classic constitutional symptom pattern (6 weeks cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats). Definitive exclusion requires sputum AFB smear and culture, which must be obtained before discharge.

history.find: Son says father attributed the breathlessness to 'getting old and too much smoking' and delayed seeking help for months. Son is worried it might be cancer. Patient, when lucid, says he mainly wants to understand why he has been so confused — it frightens him.
history.exp: The patient's attribution to ageing and smoking is extremely common in lung cancer — this is why presentations are so delayed. The son's concern about cancer is clinically astute. The patient's primary worry about his confusion is important — addressing it directly builds trust and creates an opportunity to explain that the confusion is likely from a low blood sodium caused by the lung condition. ICE is useful here for structuring the explanation of what further testing is needed and why.

pe.find: Looks unwell. Confused — disoriented to time and place. Visibly thin and malnourished; clothing appears loose. Pale. No jaundice. BILATERAL FINGER CLUBBING present. No peripheral lymphadenopathy visible. No stigmata of chronic liver disease.
pe.exp: Finger clubbing (bulbous enlargement of the distal finger pads) is associated with lung cancer, chronic pulmonary suppuration, and inflammatory bowel disease. Its presence in a heavy smoker with 3 months of haemoptysis and weight loss is a significant pointer toward malignancy. Confusion confirms central nervous system involvement — in this context, the most likely cause is metabolic (hyponatraemia from SIADH) or CNS metastases. Absence of liver disease stigmata reduces hepatic cirrhosis as a cause of dilutional hyponatraemia.
pe.lookingFor: Cachexia/malnourishment (malignancy, TB); finger clubbing (lung Ca, chronic lung disease); pallor (anaemia worsening dyspnoea); lymphadenopathy

pe.find: Temperature 37.4°C (no significant fever). Heart rate 96 bpm. Blood pressure 108/70 mmHg. Respiratory rate 22/min (elevated). SpO₂ 91% on room air. BMI estimated 17 (underweight). No postural drop in blood pressure.
pe.exp: Elevated respiratory rate and SpO₂ 91% confirm significant respiratory compromise requiring supplemental oxygen. Blood pressure is maintained at 108/70 — this argues against Addisonian crisis (which causes profound hypotension) and cardiac tamponade (which causes hypotension with pulsus paradoxus). No postural hypotension further argues against adrenal insufficiency. Temperature of 37.4°C is not significant — a higher fever would raise the concern for active TB or bacterial pneumonia.
pe.lookingFor: SpO₂ (severity of hypoxia); RR (respiratory distress); BP (tamponade → hypotension, Addison's → hypotension); HR; temperature (fever → TB, infection)

pe.find: JVP not elevated. Heart sounds: S1 and S2 present, not muffled, no murmurs, no pericardial rub. No pedal or ankle oedema. Capillary refill 2 seconds. No pulsus paradoxus detectable.
pe.exp: SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE for cardiac tamponade: Beck's triad requires raised JVP + muffled heart sounds + hypotension — all three are absent here. Absence of pulsus paradoxus (a fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg on inspiration) further argues against tamponade. Normal heart sounds without muffling or rub also reduces pericarditis. Absence of pedal oedema and raised JVP makes heart failure a less likely primary cause of the dyspnoea.
pe.lookingFor: JVP elevation (tamponade, heart failure); muffled heart sounds (tamponade); pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop on inspiration → tamponade); ankle oedema

pe.find: Trachea deviated slightly to the LEFT. Percussion DULL in the right lower and mid zones. Breath sounds REDUCED in the right lower zone. Bronchial breathing audible at right mid zone. Left lung: normal resonance and vesicular breath sounds. No wheeze.
pe.exp: Tracheal deviation to the LEFT with right-sided dullness and reduced breath sounds is the classic pattern of a large right-sided pleural effusion — the fluid bulk pushes the trachea ipsilaterally (the same side as the effusion). Note: this is the opposite of collapse or pneumothorax where the trachea deviates toward the abnormal side. Bronchial breathing at the right mid zone suggests a large central mass partially occluding the bronchus. A large pleural effusion with a central mass in a heavy smoker is highly characteristic of lung cancer.
pe.lookingFor: Tracheal deviation; dullness (effusion), stony-dull; reduced breath sounds; bronchial breathing (consolidation/mass); wheeze

pe.find: Abdomen soft. Liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin (mild hepatomegaly). Spleen not palpable. No ascites. No abdominal masses. No tenderness.
pe.exp: Mild hepatomegaly raises concern for liver metastases, which are common with SCLC and would upstage the disease to 'extensive stage.' This finding warrants LFT assessment and CT staging. Absence of ascites and splenomegaly makes portal hypertension from liver cirrhosis an unlikely cause of hyponatraemia. Absence of adrenal enlargement on examination is not clinically reliable — CT adrenal assessment is needed.
pe.lookingFor: Hepatomegaly (metastases); splenomegaly; ascites (cirrhosis causing dilutional hyponatraemia)

pe.find: RIGHT supraclavicular lymph node: approximately 1.5 cm, firm, non-tender, fixed. No axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy. No cervical lymphadenopathy.
pe.exp: A firm, non-tender, fixed supraclavicular lymph node on the right — in the context of a right-sided lung mass — is highly suspicious for locoregional lymph node metastasis of lung cancer. The right supraclavicular fossa receives drainage from the right thorax and right neck. Involvement of this node suggests at minimum N3 disease (contralateral or supraclavicular nodal involvement), which is a poor prognostic factor. This finding should prompt CT staging to fully characterise nodal involvement.
pe.lookingFor: Supraclavicular lymph nodes (lung cancer spread); axillary nodes; cervical nodes

pe.find: Skin turgor normal. Mucous membranes moist. No peripheral oedema (no ankle or sacral oedema). JVP not elevated. No orthostatic hypotension. Clinical assessment: EUVOLAEMIC — neither dehydrated nor fluid overloaded.
pe.exp: CRITICAL EXAMINATION FINDING: Euvolaemia (normal body fluid volume) with hyponatraemia is the defining clinical pattern of SIADH. Compare: hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, orthostatic hypotension) indicates sodium loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, Addison's); hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (oedema, raised JVP, ascites) indicates dilutional causes (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). Euvolaemic hyponatraemia narrows the differential significantly to SIADH, hypothyroidism, or Addison's disease. Of these, Addison's is the most dangerous and must be excluded first.
pe.lookingFor: Skin turgor; mucous membrane moisture; JVP; ankle oedema — determine volume status (euvolaemic → SIADH; hypovolaemic → sodium loss; hypervolaemic → HF/cirrhosis)

pe.find: Disoriented to time and place (GCS 13/15). No focal limb weakness — power 5/5 throughout. Reflexes normal and symmetric. No cranial nerve abnormalities. Gait unsteady but no cerebellar signs. No neck stiffness.
pe.exp: Confusion without focal neurological deficits is consistent with a diffuse metabolic cause affecting the brain globally — most likely hyponatraemia causing cerebral oedema. Absence of neck stiffness and fever reduces meningitis. No focal limb weakness makes an acute stroke less likely. However, SCLC frequently spreads to the brain — brain metastases are found in >10% of SCLC patients at diagnosis and can also cause confusion without focal deficits (if they are small or frontal). MRI brain should be performed once the patient is stabilised.
pe.lookingFor: GCS and orientation (confusion from hyponatraemia vs focal lesion vs metabolic); focal deficits (brain mets); neck stiffness (meningitis)

basic.find: Large RIGHT HILAR MASS (approximately 5 cm) at the right main bronchus. RIGHT-SIDED PLEURAL EFFUSION causing opacification of the right lower zone. Left lung clear. Trachea deviated slightly left. No pneumothorax. No rib lesions. No upper lobe consolidation or cavitation.
basic.exp: A large central hilar mass with an ipsilateral pleural effusion in a heavy smoker with haemoptysis, weight loss, and 6 weeks of progressive breathlessness is the classic CXR presentation of central lung cancer. SCLC typically arises centrally near the main airways (unlike adenocarcinoma, which is usually peripheral). Crucially, the absence of upper lobe consolidation, cavitation, or miliary shadowing makes TB less likely — though sputum AFB smear and culture are still required for definitive exclusion. This finding immediately makes lung cancer the leading diagnosis and triggers urgent CT and oncology referral.

basic.find: D-dimer: 0.41 mg/L (within normal range for this laboratory).
basic.exp: SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE: A normal D-dimer in this clinical context (subacute 6-week course, no classic acute PE risk factors) effectively excludes clinically significant pulmonary embolism as a major contributor to the breathlessness. Note: D-dimer has high sensitivity but very low specificity — it is elevated in malignancy, infection, and inflammation. Its role here is to RULE OUT PE when pre-test probability is low, not to rule it in. A positive D-dimer in a cancer patient is almost universally non-specific.

basic.find: Haemoglobin 94 g/L (low — anaemia; normal >130 g/L in men). White blood cells 12.4 × 10⁹/L (mildly elevated — non-specific). Platelets 392 × 10⁹/L (normal).
basic.exp: Anaemia (haemoglobin 94 g/L) is common in malignancy — cancer causes anaemia of chronic disease by suppressing erythropoiesis and sequestering iron. This anaemia directly worsens breathlessness by reducing oxygen-carrying capacity. Mildly elevated white count is a non-specific stress response. Normal platelets argue against haematological malignancy. The degree of anaemia here warrants consideration of IV iron or transfusion alongside cancer treatment.

basic.find: Sodium 122 mmol/L (critically low — normal 135–145 mmol/L). Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (normal). Chloride 88 mmol/L (low — mirrors hyponatraemia). Urea 2.8 mmol/L (low-normal — consistent with water retention). Creatinine 78 µmol/L (normal).
basic.exp: CRITICAL FINDING: Sodium of 122 mmol/L confirms severe hyponatraemia — this is the direct cause of the confusion (cerebral oedema begins when sodium falls below approximately 125 mmol/L). In combination with euvolaemia confirmed on examination, this is the SIADH pattern. Normal potassium is important: Addison's disease characteristically causes hyperkalaemia alongside hyponatraemia (from lack of mineralocorticoid aldosterone); normal potassium makes Addison's less likely, but it does NOT exclude it — adrenal insufficiency still needs to be excluded. Low urea reflects dilution from water retention, consistent with SIADH. This result should immediately trigger thyroid function tests, Synacthen test, and SIADH confirmation tests.

basic.find: Serum osmolality: 258 mOsm/kg (low — normal 275–295 mOsm/kg). Urine osmolality: 498 mOsm/kg (inappropriately HIGH — normal response to low serum osmolality would be very dilute urine below 100 mOsm/kg). Urine sodium: 62 mmol/L (inappropriately HIGH — should be low as kidneys try to retain sodium).
basic.exp: DIAGNOSTIC FOR SIADH: This is the confirmatory biochemical test. The paradox is: the blood is dilute (serum osmolality 258) but the urine is inappropriately concentrated (498 mOsm/kg). Normally, low serum osmolality triggers the kidneys to produce maximally dilute urine to get rid of the excess water — but in SIADH, the ectopic ADH produced by the tumour overrides this response. The formal SIADH diagnostic criteria are met: hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine + urine sodium >40 mmol/L + euvolaemia + exclusion of adrenal/thyroid causes.

basic.find: TSH 1.9 mU/L (normal). Free T4 14.8 pmol/L (normal). Thyroid function is normal.
basic.exp: Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) is a reversible cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia that must be excluded before diagnosing SIADH — hypothyroidism reduces free water clearance by a mechanism similar to SIADH. Normal TSH and free T4 here rule this out definitively. This is a mandatory exclusion test in the workup of euvolaemic hyponatraemia.

basic.find: Morning cortisol: 302 nmol/L (adequate baseline). Short ACTH stimulation test (Synacthen 250 µg IV): cortisol rises to 638 nmol/L at 30 minutes — NORMAL RESPONSE (threshold >550 nmol/L at 30 minutes). Adrenal function intact.
basic.exp: ESSENTIAL TO EXCLUDE: Addisonian crisis (adrenal insufficiency) must be actively excluded in any patient with euvolaemic hyponatraemia — it is immediately life-threatening and reversible with hydrocortisone replacement. An adrenal crisis can present identically to SIADH biochemically (low sodium, euvolaemia) but requires completely different and urgent treatment. A 9 am serum cortisol checked early, with a Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test when appropriate, confirms the adrenal glands are working and allows SIADH to be diagnosed with confidence. Exclude adrenal insufficiency before attributing the hyponatraemia to SIADH.

basic.find: ALT 58 U/L (mildly elevated). AST 52 U/L (mildly elevated). ALP 162 U/L (elevated). Albumin 25 g/L (low — normal >35 g/L). Bilirubin 13 µmol/L (normal).
basic.exp: Mildly elevated transaminases and ALP suggest hepatic involvement — consistent with liver metastases given the hepatomegaly on examination. Low albumin reflects malnutrition from malignancy (cancer cachexia). These findings support advanced disease and warrant CT staging. Note: hepatic cirrhosis causes dilutional hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (with oedema and ascites) — not the euvolaemic pattern seen here; these LFT abnormalities are from metastatic disease, not cirrhosis.

basic.find: AFB smear: NEGATIVE (no acid-fast bacilli seen). Sputum culture: no bacterial growth at 48 hours; TB culture pending (8 weeks). Sputum cytology: MALIGNANT CELLS identified — small cells with scant cytoplasm, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and stippled chromatin. Morphology consistent with small cell carcinoma.
basic.exp: Sputum testing serves two purposes simultaneously: (1) AFB smear and culture to exclude TB — the negative smear reduces infectious TB probability, though culture (8 weeks) is the gold standard. Patients with suspected TB should be isolated pending results. (2) Cytology — finding malignant SCLC cells in sputum confirms the diagnosis non-invasively. The classic description of 'small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and stippled chromatin' is the morphological hallmark of SCLC.

basic.find: pH 7.38 (normal). PaO₂ 8.1 kPa (low — normal >10 kPa on room air = Type 1 respiratory failure). PaCO₂ 5.0 kPa (normal). HCO₃ 22 mmol/L (normal). Lactate 1.7 mmol/L (normal).
basic.exp: Type 1 respiratory failure (low PaO₂ without CO₂ retention) indicates impaired gas exchange at the alveolar level, consistent with pleural effusion, malignant consolidation, and tumour mass reducing functional lung volume. Type 2 failure (elevated PaCO₂) would suggest ventilatory failure as in severe COPD exacerbation — absent here. Normal lactate argues against cardiogenic shock or severe sepsis. Supplemental oxygen is required and should be titrated to SpO₂ 94–98%.

advanced.find: Right hilar mass (5.3 × 5.1 cm) at the right main bronchus with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (N2/N3 nodes). Moderate right pleural effusion. Multiple hepatic hypodense lesions consistent with metastases (largest 1.9 cm). Adrenal glands appear normal. No bony metastases identified on this scan. No upper lobe cavitation or miliary pattern (TB unlikely but not excluded).
advanced.exp: CT confirms extensive disease: large central lung mass, mediastinal nodal involvement, hepatic metastases, and pleural effusion. In SCLC staging, this is 'extensive stage' disease (beyond one hemithorax), which occurs in 60–70% of SCLC patients at diagnosis. Hepatic metastases explain the elevated ALP and hepatomegaly. Normal adrenals are consistent with the normal Synacthen test. Absence of upper lobe cavitation or miliary pattern reduces TB probability, though sputum culture remains the definitive exclusion. Brain MRI is required separately for SCLC staging.

advanced.find: Bronchoscopy: right main bronchus almost completely obstructed by an endobronchial tumour. Biopsy: SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER (SCLC). Histology: dense sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 positive, synaptophysin positive, CD56 positive, Ki-67 >80% (very high proliferative rate — characteristic of SCLC).
advanced.exp: Bronchoscopy with tissue biopsy is the gold standard for central lung tumour diagnosis. The histological features confirm SCLC: small cells with neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, CD56, TTF-1) and an extremely high Ki-67 proliferative index (>80% is typical for SCLC — one of the fastest-dividing cancers). These same neuroendocrine cells produce ectopic ADH, causing the paraneoplastic SIADH. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid sent for TB culture provides an additional sample alongside sputum.

advanced.find: Two small enhancing lesions: right frontal lobe (1.0 cm) and right cerebellar hemisphere (0.8 cm). Consistent with brain metastases. No significant oedema or midline shift.
advanced.exp: Brain metastases are found in >10% of SCLC patients at initial diagnosis and ultimately develop in up to 80% of patients over the disease course. MRI brain is more sensitive than CT for detecting small brain metastases and is recommended in all SCLC patients at staging. Finding brain metastases confirms extensive stage disease. They may also contribute to the confusion alongside the hyponatraemia. Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is considered in patients achieving complete remission.

advanced.find: 450 mL straw-coloured fluid aspirated. Exudate (protein elevated, meets Light's criteria). Cytology: malignant cells consistent with SCLC. Culture: negative. AFB smear: negative.
advanced.exp: Pleural fluid aspiration serves two purposes: (1) diagnostic — malignant cells confirm pleural spread of SCLC (upstages to extensive disease), and negative AFB smear further reduces pleural TB; (2) therapeutic — removing 450 mL of fluid immediately improves breathing and oxygen saturation. Malignant pleural effusion indicates systemic chemotherapy is the primary treatment. Note: even a negative pleural cytology does not exclude malignant effusion — sensitivity is approximately 60% for a single sample.

advanced.find: Not performed — CT staging and MRI brain completed; extensive stage SCLC confirmed without PET-CT.
advanced.exp: PET-CT uses radioactive glucose tracer to identify metabolically active tissue including cancer spread. For SCLC, the staging system is simpler than non-SCLC (limited stage vs extensive stage), and CT plus MRI brain is generally sufficient for staging. PET-CT may assist in limited-stage SCLC to define the radiotherapy field, but is not routinely required in obvious extensive stage disease where hepatic and brain metastases are already confirmed.

cases.secondaryDxLabel: Paraneoplastic SIADH (from SCLC producing ectopic ADH)

linkedPairs.note: SIADH is a paraneoplastic complication of SCLC — it cannot be ranked above the cancer causing it

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: No raised JVP, no muffled heart sounds, BP maintained — Beck's triad absent, tamponade unlikely
Normal D-dimer with subacute 6-week course and no acute PE risk factors — PE effectively excluded
Normal Synacthen test — adrenal function confirmed intact, Addison's excluded
Sputum cytology: malignant SCLC cells, no AFB seen — primary diagnosis is SCLC. TB culture pending but SCLC is confirmed

cases.title: Worsening Headache with Arm Weakness
cases.secondaryApproach: An Approach to Focal Neurological Deficit
cases.patient: Miss Chen Mei Ling, 28F, Primary School Teacher

validation.notes: Awaiting neurology sign-off on imaging sequence.

reasoning.bi02: A normal plain CT head does NOT exclude CVST — proceed to CT/MR venography when suspicion remains.
reasoning.subarachnoid_haemorrhage_sah: Thunderclap onset would mandate urgent CT ± LP — kept as the headache safety net.

cases.vignette: Miss Chen Mei Ling is a 28-year-old primary school teacher who presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of progressively worsening headache. The headache has not responded to paracetamol. This morning, she noticed weakness in her left arm while writing on the whiteboard.

sigNegs.label: Normal CRP and WBC → bacterial meningitis and brain abscess very unlikely
No neck stiffness, no photophobia → reduces meningitis probability significantly
CT head: no subarachnoid blood → SAH excluded on imaging; subtle dense sinus sign noted
LP: clear CSF, no xanthochromia, elevated opening pressure → SAH excluded, raised ICP confirmed

keyTeachingPoints: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) is a blood clot in the large veins that drain blood from the brain. Unlike arterial stroke, it typically presents with a progressively worsening headache over days, making it easy to miss and misdiagnose as migraine.

The oral contraceptive pill (OCP) is the most important risk factor for CVST in young women. Oestrogen in the combined OCP increases clotting tendency (prothrombotic effect) by 3-6 times. Any young woman on OCP presenting with an unusual or progressive headache should have CVST considered.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) — bleeding around the brain from a ruptured aneurysm — is the most dangerous must-not-miss diagnosis for any severe headache. SAH typically presents as a 'thunderclap headache' (worst headache of life, maximal within seconds). CT head within 6 hours has ~95% sensitivity; if negative, lumbar puncture is required.

Meningitis must always be considered in anyone with headache. The classic triad is headache, fever, and neck stiffness — but not all features are always present. A non-blanching purpuric rash is a dermatological emergency requiring immediate IV antibiotics.

CVST can cause focal neurological deficits (like the left arm weakness in this case) because blocked venous drainage causes brain swelling and localised venous ischaemia — affecting the cortex served by the obstructed sinus.

MRI with MR venography (MRV) is the gold-standard investigation for CVST. CT head and CT angiography can be normal or show only subtle signs. The absence of blood on a regular CT does not exclude CVST — and should not falsely reassure if clinical suspicion remains.

Treatment of CVST is anticoagulation (blood thinners), even in the presence of haemorrhage on imaging — this is counterintuitive but supported by evidence. The OCP should be stopped immediately. Prognosis is generally good if diagnosed early.

Primary headaches (migraine, tension-type headache) are diagnoses of exclusion — dangerous secondary causes must be excluded first. Red flags that mandate investigation: new/worst headache, progressive headache, focal neurological deficit, papilloedema, fever, altered consciousness, or known cancer/immunocompromise.

findings.text: Headache is progressive over 5 days — SAH classically presents as 'thunderclap' (worst headache of life, maximal within seconds of onset, not gradually worsening)
CT head: no subarachnoid blood in cisterns or sulci — CT within 6 hours has ~95% sensitivity for SAH
Lumbar puncture: CSF colourless and clear, no xanthochromia (yellow staining from blood breakdown products), no red blood cells — excludes SAH definitively
No fever, no recent infection, no immunosuppression — classic risk factors for bacterial meningitis absent
No neck stiffness (Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs negative). No photophobia. No purpuric rash on skin examination.
Normal CRP and white cell count — bacterial meningitis causes a marked systemic inflammatory response; normal inflammatory markers make it very unlikely
CSF analysis: clear fluid, normal glucose ratio (>0.6), normal protein, no organisms on Gram stain, no white cells — excludes bacterial and viral meningitis

mnmRuleOut.statusLbl: Excluded — this is venous, not arterial

findings.text: Gradual onset headache over 5 days before focal deficit — arterial stroke typically causes sudden onset focal deficit without days of prodromal headache
CT head: no arterial territory infarct. MRI DWI: no restricted diffusion in an arterial territory — rules out arterial ischaemic stroke
MR venography: absent flow signal in superior sagittal sinus and right transverse sinus — confirms venous (not arterial) thrombosis as the cause of the focal deficit
Blood pressure 134/86 mmHg — elevated but not in hypertensive emergency range (>180/120 mmHg with end-organ damage)
No papilloedema on fundoscopy attributable to hypertension — the papilloedema here is from raised ICP due to venous obstruction, not hypertensive retinopathy
No prior history of hypertension. Young patient. Mild BP elevation is likely reactive to pain and raised ICP rather than the primary cause.

cases.approachSub: Reference: Nigel Fong, Algorithms in Differential Diagnosis
cases.approachText: The key principle in headache is distinguishing dangerous secondary headaches (caused by a serious underlying condition) from benign primary headaches (no underlying disease). Red flags identify secondary headaches that must not be missed:

approachCats.name: Vascular — Clot ← THIS CASE
approachCats.eg: CVST, ischaemic stroke, TIA, carotid artery dissection

approachCats.name: Infectious / Inflammatory
approachCats.eg: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, TB meningitis, brain abscess, encephalitis

approachCats.name: Raised Intracranial Pressure
approachCats.eg: Brain tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, hydrocephalus

approachCats.name: Primary Headaches (diagnosis of exclusion)
approachCats.eg: Migraine, tension-type headache, cluster headache — only after dangerous causes excluded

cases.approachInsight: CVST is the classic 'dangerous diagnosis masquerading as a primary headache.' It presents with a progressive headache that can be misdiagnosed as migraine for days. The RED FLAGS that should prompt urgent investigation are: (1) Progressive worsening despite treatment, (2) New focal neurological deficit, (3) OCP use or other prothrombotic risk factors — identified in drug history, (4) Papilloedema on fundoscopy. The critical lesson: migraine and tension headache are diagnoses of EXCLUSION — you must first rule out all dangerous secondary causes.
cases.expertNarrative: CVST in a young woman on the combined OCP is the classic presentation. Oestrogen in the OCP increases clotting factor activity, reducing natural anticoagulant protein S activity and raising the risk of venous thrombosis by 3-6 times. Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus and transverse sinus obstructs venous outflow from the brain, causing raised intracranial pressure (explaining the progressive headache and papilloedema) and cortical venous congestion/ischaemia (explaining the focal left arm weakness from right parietal lobe involvement). The key diagnostic insight: unlike SAH (thunderclap, maximal at onset) or arterial stroke (sudden focal deficit, no headache prodrome), CVST is subacute and progressive over days. It requires MR venography for diagnosis — a normal CT head does not exclude it. Treatment is anticoagulation. The antiphospholipid antibody screen was positive here, identifying an additional prothrombotic risk factor that was amplified by OCP use.
cases.sensitivityNote: CVST is poorly sensitive for a 'classic' headache presentation — it is subacute, progressive, and mimics migraine. Headache occurs in ~90% of cases but its character is variable. A high index of suspicion is required in young women on OCP with unusual or progressive headache. CT head and LP may be normal — MR venography is the essential investigation.
cases.specificityNote: MR venography showing absent flow in a dural venous sinus (e.g. superior sagittal sinus, transverse sinus) is highly specific for CVST. The 'empty delta sign' on CT with contrast (filling defect in the sinus where there should be enhancing flowing blood, surrounded by enhancing walls) is also specific but less sensitive (~30%). D-dimer elevation supports the diagnosis but is not specific.

history.find: Headache started 5 days ago, gradual onset, progressively worsening each day. Now 8/10 severity. Located over the top of the head and behind both eyes — diffuse, bilateral. Pressure-like and throbbing quality. NOT 'the worst of her life' and did NOT start suddenly at maximum intensity.
history.exp: The GRADUALLY PROGRESSIVE onset over 5 days is the key distinguishing feature from SAH (which is thunderclap — maximal intensity within seconds of onset). A headache that is new, atypical, and worsening daily — especially in a patient with risk factors — is a red flag that mandates investigation. The bilateral, progressive nature over days is the characteristic pattern of CVST, which causes raised intracranial pressure as venous outflow is obstructed.

history.find: Left arm weakness noticed this morning while writing on the whiteboard — unable to write normally. No leg weakness. No speech difficulty. No facial drooping. Bilateral blurred vision for the past 2 days (not one-sided visual loss).
history.exp: Left arm weakness is a focal neurological deficit — this is a critical red flag that immediately removes this from the category of primary headache (migraine, tension). Focal deficits occur in approximately 40% of CVST patients due to venous congestion causing cortical ischaemia. Bilateral blurred vision in the context of a headache raises concern for papilloedema (swelling of the optic nerve head from raised intracranial pressure) rather than unilateral visual loss from retinal ischaemia. Together, progressive headache + focal deficit mandates emergency imaging.

history.find: Nausea and two episodes of vomiting over the past 2 days. No fever. No rash. No photophobia. No phonophobia.
history.exp: Nausea and vomiting with headache can occur in migraine, raised intracranial pressure, and meningitis. Absence of fever and rash reduces bacterial meningitis likelihood. Absence of photophobia and phonophobia reduces (but does not exclude) migraine with aura. The key point: the 5-day progressive course with worsening vomiting is not typical for episodic migraine. Vomiting from raised intracranial pressure tends to be projectile and occurs without nausea — though this distinction is not reliable clinically.

history.find: Has had occasional migraines since university — typically right-sided, with flashing lights (aura) beforehand, responding well to sumatriptan and rest. This current headache feels completely DIFFERENT — bilateral, no aura, not responding to her usual migraine medication, and getting worse every day for 5 days.
history.exp: This is a critically important piece of history: the patient herself recognises this headache as DIFFERENT from her usual migraines. 'A new, different, or worst headache' is the most important red flag in headache assessment. The lack of response to her usual migraine treatment is another red flag. This history rules out 'just another migraine' — a different diagnosis must be sought. Any patient with a change in headache pattern or a headache that does not behave like their usual migraines requires investigation.

history.find: Started the combined oral contraceptive pill (Microgynon 30 — contains oestrogen and progesterone) 4 months ago. Sumatriptan (for migraines) as needed. Paracetamol — not helping with this headache. No other regular medications. No known drug allergies.
history.exp: CRITICAL PIECE OF HISTORY: The combined oral contraceptive pill (combined OCP) is the most important risk factor for CVST in young women. Oestrogen in the combined OCP increases thrombotic risk by 3-6 times by raising clotting factor levels and reducing protein S activity. Starting OCP 4 months ago is very clinically relevant — CVST can develop at any time during OCP use. The OCP must be stopped immediately once CVST is confirmed. This information would NOT be known if drug history were not specifically taken.

history.find: No prior neurological conditions. No prior blood clots (DVT or PE). No recent surgery or prolonged immobility. No known clotting disorders. No cancer. No autoimmune disease.
history.exp: Absence of prior DVT, PE, and known thrombophilia reduces (but does not exclude) inherited clotting tendency. The OCP alone is sufficient as a risk factor for CVST. However, an underlying thrombophilia (such as antiphospholipid syndrome, Factor V Leiden, or protein C/S deficiency) combined with OCP use substantially amplifies the risk. Thrombophilia screen is warranted after the acute event is managed.

history.lbl: Family history of blood clots or stroke
history.find: Mother had a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in her leg at age 38. No other family history of clots, strokes, or neurological conditions. No family history of autoimmune disease.
history.exp: Family history of DVT in the mother at a young age raises the possibility of an inherited thrombophilia — a hereditary tendency to form blood clots. Common inherited thrombophilias include Factor V Leiden (most common), prothrombin gene mutation, and antithrombin/protein C/S deficiency. This history makes antiphospholipid syndrome or an inherited thrombophilia more likely, and substantially increases CVST risk when combined with OCP use. Thrombophilia screening should be arranged.

history.find: Last menstrual period 3 weeks ago (normal cycle on OCP). Not pregnant (urine pregnancy test negative in triage). No prior pregnancies. No history of miscarriage.
history.exp: Confirming she is not pregnant is essential — pregnancy is itself a high-risk period for CVST (particularly in the third trimester and postpartum). A negative pregnancy test allows full investigation including CT/MRI with contrast without obstetric concern. No prior miscarriage reduces the clinical likelihood of antiphospholipid syndrome, though a single negative test does not exclude it — antiphospholipid antibody testing should still be sent.

history.find: Non-smoker. Occasional alcohol (1-2 glasses per week). Works as a primary school teacher. No illicit drug use.
