history.exp: Smoking is a prothrombotic risk factor — reassuringly absent here. Drug use (cocaine, amphetamines) can cause cerebral vasospasm and haemorrhagic stroke in young people — absence noted. Absence of additional cardiovascular risk factors is consistent with the young, otherwise healthy profile. The primary risk factors in this case are OCP use and the family history suggesting possible inherited thrombophilia.

history.lbl: Systemic review — fever, rash, joint pains
history.find: No fever. No recent infection. No rash (no purpura, no malar rash). No oral ulcers. No joint pains or swellings. No dry eyes or dry mouth.
history.exp: Absence of fever and rash reduces infectious meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia. Absence of oral ulcers, malar rash, and joint pains reduces SLE — an autoimmune disease associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, which is a recognised cause of CVST in young women. However, antiphospholipid syndrome must still be screened for with specific blood tests even in the absence of these features.

history.find: She initially thought she had a 'very bad migraine' and hoped for stronger migraine medication. She is now frightened because the arm weakness has alarmed her — she has never had this before. She wants to know what is wrong and whether it is serious.
history.exp: ICE is important here. Her initial interpretation as migraine is understandable given her history — but it delayed her presentation by 4 days. Her fear at the focal neurological deficit is clinically appropriate and represents a correct alarm signal. Communicating clearly and empathetically about the need for urgent imaging is essential. Her expectation of 'stronger migraine tablets' needs to be redirected — this is not a migraine, and the management is fundamentally different.

pe.find: Looks distressed and in pain, holding her head. Alert and oriented to person, place, and time (GCS 15). No rash anywhere on the body — no petechiae, no purpura. No facial asymmetry at rest.
pe.exp: Preserved consciousness (GCS 15) is reassuring against rapidly rising intracranial pressure causing imminent herniation. Actively inspecting for a non-blanching purpuric rash is essential in anyone with headache — the rash of meningococcal septicaemia is a dermatological emergency: if found, IV benzylpenicillin should be given immediately before any other investigation. Absence of rash is an important negative finding.
pe.lookingFor: GCS level; non-blanching purpuric rash anywhere on body (meningococcal septicaemia → immediate IV penicillin); photophobia

pe.find: Temperature 37.2°C (no fever). Blood pressure 134/86 mmHg (mildly elevated). Heart rate 88 bpm. Breathing rate 16/min. Oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
pe.exp: No fever — important negative against infectious meningitis and encephalitis. Mildly elevated blood pressure may be reactive (pain, anxiety) or represent Cushing's reflex (raised BP + bradycardia) from raised intracranial pressure — though true Cushing's reflex indicates imminent herniation. Not in hypertensive emergency range (>180/120 mmHg with end-organ damage). Normal oxygen saturation is reassuring.
pe.lookingFor: BP (>180/120 with symptoms → hypertensive emergency; Cushing's reflex = raised BP + bradycardia → impending herniation); temperature (fever → meningitis/encephalitis)

pe.lbl: Fundoscopy (examining the back of the eye)
pe.find: BILATERAL PAPILLOEDEMA — blurring and elevation of both optic disc margins, with loss of spontaneous venous pulsations. No retinal haemorrhages.
pe.exp: Papilloedema (swelling of the optic nerve head visible at the back of the eye) is caused by raised intracranial pressure — the increased pressure inside the skull is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath. Bilateral papilloedema in a young woman with progressive headache, visual changes, and focal neurological deficit is a critical clinical finding that demands urgent brain imaging. It confirms genuinely raised intracranial pressure from any cause (venous thrombosis, tumour, IIH, etc.).
pe.lookingFor: Optic disc margins — blurring and elevation = papilloedema = raised ICP; loss of venous pulsations (earliest sign); haemorrhages

pe.find: Neck stiffness: ABSENT — full range of neck movement without pain. Kernig's sign: NEGATIVE (can straighten the knee with hip flexed to 90°). Brudzinski's sign: NEGATIVE. No photophobia on direct examination. No phonophobia.
pe.exp: SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE: Absence of meningism (neck stiffness, positive Kernig's/Brudzinski's) significantly reduces bacterial meningitis probability. These signs result from irritation of the meningeal lining by infection or blood. However, meningism can be absent in early meningitis — if clinical suspicion remains, CSF examination is still required. In this case, normal inflammatory markers (CRP, WBC) provide further reassurance against bacterial meningitis.
pe.lookingFor: Neck stiffness (meningism); Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension with hip at 90°); Brudzinski's (neck flexion causes hip flexion); photophobia; phonophobia

pe.find: LEFT arm: power 3/5 (moderately weak — cannot overcome gravity fully). Left arm reflexes brisk. Left-sided coordination impaired (finger-nose test). RIGHT arm: power 5/5 (normal). Both legs: power 5/5. LEFT plantar reflex: UPGOING (Babinski sign positive — indicates upper motor neuron dysfunction). Sensation intact bilaterally.
pe.exp: Left-sided upper limb weakness with brisk reflexes and an upgoing Babinski sign indicates an UPPER MOTOR NEURON (UMN) lesion in the RIGHT cerebral hemisphere (the right brain controls the left side of the body). This localises the injury to the right cortex or right corticospinal tract. In CVST, this occurs because thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus causes venous hypertension and ischaemia in the right parietal cortex — the area controlling left arm movement. This pattern distinguishes cerebral pathology from a peripheral nerve lesion.
pe.lookingFor: Power, tone, reflexes in all 4 limbs; plantar response (upgoing = UMN lesion); coordination; distinguish focal (cortical lesion) from global (metabolic)

pe.find: Visual fields: full to confrontation in both eyes. Visual acuity: 6/6 bilaterally. Colour vision normal.
pe.exp: Full visual fields argue against homonymous hemianopia (loss of half the visual field on one side), which would suggest a posterior cerebral lesion (occipital lobe or optic radiation involvement). Normal visual acuity despite papilloedema is expected in early raised ICP — sustained high pressure eventually damages the optic nerves, but this is a late complication. The bilateral blurred vision the patient described is more consistent with papilloedema-related optical distortion than a field cut.
pe.lookingFor: Visual field confrontation testing (hemianopia → posterior cerebral lesion); visual acuity (papilloedema-related blurring); colour vision

pe.find: No rash on any body surface — no petechiae (tiny red dots), no purpura (larger purple spots). Normal skin turgor. No oral ulcers or mucosal lesions.
pe.exp: A thorough skin examination for non-blanching purpuric rash is mandatory in any patient presenting with headache. The rash of meningococcal septicaemia requires immediate IV penicillin before any investigation — the rash is the trigger to act, not CT or blood tests. Absence of rash is reassuring. Absence of oral ulcers reduces Behçet's disease (a vasculitis that causes both oral ulcers and CVST).
pe.lookingFor: Active search for non-blanching purpuric rash on all skin surfaces; oral ulcers (Behçet's disease → CVST); petechiae

pe.find: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs. Lungs clear. No signs of heart failure. Regular rhythm.
pe.exp: A baseline cardiovascular examination is reasonable in any neurological presentation. Absence of murmurs reduces the risk of infective endocarditis with septic emboli as a cause of the neurological signs — an uncommon but important cause of stroke in young people. Not a discriminating examination in this specific case.
pe.lookingFor: Murmurs (infective endocarditis → septic emboli → stroke in young); cardiac rhythm; evidence of heart failure

basic.find: White blood cells: 8.4 × 10⁹/L (normal). Haemoglobin 128 g/L (mildly low). Platelets 292 × 10⁹/L (normal). CRP: 7 mg/L (normal).
basic.exp: SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE: Normal white cell count and CRP make bacterial meningitis and brain abscess very unlikely — these conditions cause a marked systemic inflammatory response with elevated WBC and CRP. Mildly low haemoglobin may reflect iron deficiency. Normal platelet count argues against thrombocytopenia-related thrombosis. Combined with absent meningism on examination, normal inflammatory markers effectively exclude bacterial meningitis.

basic.find: No subarachnoid blood. No intracerebral haemorrhage. No midline shift. No obvious hypodense infarct. Subtle HYPERDENSITY (whiteness) noted in the superior sagittal sinus — possible 'dense sinus sign', suggesting the sinus contains thrombosed (clotted) rather than flowing blood. No evidence of raised ICP on CT.
basic.exp: CT head is essential to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage (which appears as bright white blood in the subarachnoid space) and intracranial haemorrhage. Absence of subarachnoid blood effectively excludes SAH (sensitivity ~95% within 6 hours of onset). The subtle 'dense sinus sign' — the venous sinus appearing whiter than usual on non-contrast CT — is an indirect CT sign of venous sinus thrombosis, but it is subtle and easily missed on CT alone. CT head alone is INSUFFICIENT to confirm or exclude CVST — MR venography is required.

basic.find: Prothrombin time (PT/INR): normal. APTT: normal. Fibrinogen: 4.1 g/L (normal).
basic.exp: Basic clotting tests are important before any invasive procedure (lumbar puncture, anticoagulation). Normal coagulation profile means anticoagulation can be started safely. Note: antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies) are a specific cause of CVST and require dedicated testing — they are NOT detected by standard coagulation screens.

basic.find: Sodium 139 mmol/L (normal). All other electrolytes and renal function within normal range.
basic.exp: Normal electrolytes make metabolic causes of confusion (hyponatraemia, uraemia) unlikely. Useful pre-treatment baseline, but not a discriminating investigation in this case. Normal sodium is consistent with CVST, where confusion arises from focal cerebral ischaemia rather than metabolic derangement.

basic.find: Urine beta-hCG: NEGATIVE. Not pregnant.
basic.exp: A pregnancy test is mandatory in any woman of childbearing age before CT/MRI with contrast and before starting anticoagulation. Pregnancy is a high-risk period for CVST, particularly in the third trimester and postpartum. A negative result allows full imaging and treatment without obstetric complication.

basic.find: D-dimer: 2.6 mg/L (elevated — above upper limit of normal).
basic.exp: An elevated D-dimer is consistent with active thrombosis anywhere in the body, including CVST. D-dimer is not specific for CVST and is elevated in many other conditions. However, in a patient with risk factors and clinical features of CVST, an elevated D-dimer provides supporting evidence. A NORMAL D-dimer in a low-risk patient would reduce the probability of CVST, but a normal D-dimer does NOT exclude CVST in a high-risk patient — imaging is still required.

basic.find: Opening pressure: 28 cmH₂O (ELEVATED — normal under 20 cmH₂O). CSF appearance: clear, colourless fluid. No red blood cells. No white blood cells. Protein: normal. Glucose ratio: >0.6 (normal). No organisms on Gram stain. Xanthochromia: NEGATIVE.
basic.exp: LP is essential to exclude SAH when CT head is negative but suspicion remains (LP should always be done AFTER CT to exclude a mass lesion that would make LP dangerous). The ELEVATED opening pressure (28 cmH₂O) confirms raised intracranial pressure — consistent with CVST obstructing venous drainage from the brain. Clear, colourless CSF with no blood and NEGATIVE xanthochromia definitively excludes SAH. Normal glucose, no white cells, and no organisms exclude both bacterial and viral meningitis. The raised opening pressure is the key LP finding here.

basic.find: Antiphospholipid antibodies: POSITIVE — lupus anticoagulant detected. Anticardiolipin IgG: 52 GPL units (elevated, above 40 units). Factor V Leiden: NEGATIVE. Prothrombin gene mutation: NEGATIVE. Protein C and S: normal (note: may be transiently low on anticoagulation — repeat off treatment).
basic.exp: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune prothrombotic condition. Diagnosis requires positive tests on TWO occasions 12 weeks apart — this positive result needs to be confirmed. Finding antiphospholipid antibodies in a young woman with CVST is very significant: it means the OCP triggered CVST in a patient already predisposed to clotting. APS requires long-term anticoagulation and the combined OCP is permanently contraindicated. This explains the family history of early DVT — the mother likely also has APS or an inherited thrombophilia.

advanced.find: MRI brain: area of T2 signal change (oedema/early venous infarction) in the right parietal lobe — consistent with venous congestion from obstructed drainage. MR venography: ABSENT FLOW SIGNAL in the superior sagittal sinus (SSS) and right transverse sinus. All other sinuses show normal flow. CONFIRMS CEREBRAL VENOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS involving the SSS and right transverse sinus.
advanced.exp: MRI with MR venography (MRV) is the GOLD STANDARD investigation for CVST. MRV specifically examines blood flow in the large venous sinuses — absent flow signal confirms thrombosis. The superior sagittal sinus (SSS) is the most commonly affected sinus in CVST. The right parietal lobe signal change explains the left arm weakness (right hemisphere controls left body movement). This investigation clinches the diagnosis and guides treatment. MRV should be performed in any patient with suspected CVST after CT head has excluded haemorrhage.

advanced.find: CT venography: 'Empty delta sign' present in the superior sagittal sinus — triangular filling defect (non-enhancing clot) surrounded by enhancing sinus walls. Confirms superior sagittal sinus thrombosis. Findings correlate with MR venography.
advanced.exp: CT venography is an alternative to MR venography when MRI is contraindicated. The 'empty delta sign' (a triangular filling defect in the posterior SSS on contrast CT) is a classic finding of CVST — though it is seen in only ~30% of cases and absence does not exclude CVST. When present, it is highly specific. Combined with MRV, this provides high-confidence confirmation. CT venography is faster than MRI and may be preferred in unstable patients.

advanced.find: Right parietal lobe: T2/FLAIR signal change and mild restricted diffusion (early venous infarction/oedema). No ring-enhancing lesions (excludes brain abscess). No leptomeningeal enhancement (argues against meningitis). Findings are in the right parietal cortex in the drainage territory of the superior sagittal sinus.
advanced.exp: MRI with contrast adds information about the extent of brain injury from the CVST. The right parietal signal change — in the SSS drainage territory — explains the left arm weakness (right parietal lobe controls left arm). Absence of ring-enhancing lesions excludes brain abscess. Absence of leptomeningeal enhancement argues against meningitis. Understanding which drainage territory is affected helps predict the clinical deficits.

advanced.find: CT angiography: cerebral arteries normal throughout. No arterial occlusion, no aneurysm, no arteriovenous malformation.
advanced.exp: CT angiography examines the brain ARTERIES — it is used to look for arterial stroke (arterial occlusion) or SAH source (aneurysm). In CVST, the arteries are normal — the problem is in the veins. Ordering CT angiography here reflects a failure to distinguish between arterial stroke and venous thrombosis. MR venography was the correct investigation. This is a common error when the concept of venous vs arterial stroke is not well understood.

advanced.find: Slowing of electrical activity over the right hemisphere — consistent with focal brain dysfunction. No epileptiform discharges at the time of recording.
advanced.exp: EEG measures brain electrical activity and is primarily useful for diagnosing epilepsy. CVST can cause seizures (in 20-40% of patients), and EEG would be important if the patient had a seizure or if subclinical seizures were suspected. However, ordering EEG as a first-line investigation before confirming the diagnosis with venography is not the priority. It would be used to monitor for seizure activity after the diagnosis is established.

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: No neck stiffness, no meningism, no fever — meningitis significantly less likely
BP 134/86 mmHg — elevated but well below hypertensive emergency threshold of >180/120 mmHg with end-organ damage
CT head: no subarachnoid blood — SAH excluded on imaging (sensitivity ~95% within 6 hours)
LP: no xanthochromia, no red blood cells — SAH definitively excluded
Normal WBC and CRP — bacterial meningitis causes marked systemic inflammatory response; normal markers effectively exclude it
MR venography confirms CVST (venous thrombosis) — this is venous, not arterial; arterial ischaemic stroke excluded by MRI DWI

validation.notes: Awaiting neurology sign-off on antibody/electrophysiology sequence.

reasoning.pe06: Bedside single-breath count is the fastest airway screen — a falling count flags impending crisis before SpO2 drops.
reasoning.bi01: Formal FVC first among investigations: it is the number that decides ICU vs ward (the 20/30/40 rule), not the antibody result.
reasoning.ai01: Anti-AChR antibody is the confirmatory discriminator and is withheld to this stage; RNS/SFEMG and CT thorax follow to characterise and screen for thymoma.
reasoning.myasthenia_gravis: Fatigable ptosis + normal pupils + preserved reflexes localise to the neuromuscular junction; antibodies and decrement confirm.

cases.vignette: Ms Siti Rahimah is a 30-year-old accountant who presents with a 3-week history of a drooping right eyelid and intermittent double vision. She has noticed that both are barely there when she wakes but become more obvious as the day goes on, particularly after long stretches at her computer.

history.find: Right upper eyelid droops; horizontal double vision that comes and goes. Both are minimal on waking and after a nap, and worsen progressively through the day — worst in the evening and after reading or screen work. Resting the eyes for a few minutes makes the lid lift again.
history.exp: Fatigability with a clear diurnal pattern — better after rest, worse with sustained use and towards the end of the day — is the single most useful pointer to a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder. A fixed, non-fluctuating deficit would point elsewhere (e.g. a structural cranial nerve lesion).

history.find: Her voice fades and becomes nasal towards the end of long phone calls, and her jaw tires partway through a meal so she stops chewing to rest. No frank choking on fluids, no nasal regurgitation of liquids.
history.exp: Fatigable bulbar weakness (voice fading, jaw tiring mid-meal) signals spread beyond the eyes and raises the stakes — bulbar and respiratory involvement are what make MG a must-not-miss, because they herald aspiration and crisis.

history.find: No breathlessness at rest and no orthopnoea. She does feel slightly “short of puff” climbing stairs late in the evening but can lie flat comfortably and sleep through the night.
history.exp: Orthopnoea and exertional breathlessness that worsen with fatigue are early signs of diaphragmatic weakness. Their absence is reassuring now, but respiratory function must still be measured — oxygen desaturation is a late sign in neuromuscular respiratory failure.

history.find: Her arms tire when hanging out laundry or combing her hair, and her legs feel heavier climbing stairs late in the day. Strength is near-normal in the morning. The weakness is proximal and fluctuates rather than steadily progressing.
history.exp: Proximal, fatigable, fluctuating limb weakness fits generalised MG. The morning–evening swing again separates an NMJ disorder from a fixed structural or steadily progressive cause.

history.lbl: Speed of onset and time course
history.find: Symptoms came on gradually over about three weeks and fluctuate day to day. Nothing started suddenly or “all at once.”
history.exp: A gradual, fluctuating course over weeks argues strongly against a brainstem stroke, which is sudden (maximal at onset). Tempo is one of the cheapest and most powerful discriminators in neurology.

history.lbl: Symptoms with use, dry mouth, autonomic features
history.find: Sustained activity makes her weaker, and rest helps — she does NOT transiently improve with exercise. No dry mouth, no constipation, no light-headedness on standing.
history.exp: This is the Lambert-Eaton (LEMS) screen. LEMS classically improves transiently with sustained effort (post-exercise facilitation) and carries autonomic features (dry mouth, constipation) plus a small-cell lung cancer association. MG does the opposite — it fatigues with use.

history.find: No heat intolerance, no palpitations, weight stable, no neck swelling or gritty/protruding eyes.
history.exp: Thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy) can also cause lid and ocular-motility problems. The absence of thyrotoxic features makes it less likely — but autoimmune thyroid disease coexists with MG, so thyroid function is still checked before treatment.

history.lbl: Drug history, allergies, preceding infection, exposures
history.find: No regular medications and no drug allergies (NKDA). No recent diarrhoeal or respiratory illness, no home-canned or fermented foods, and no wounds. Family history notable for a sister with autoimmune hypothyroidism.
history.exp: A preceding gastrointestinal/respiratory infection would raise Guillain–Barré (including the Miller-Fisher variant); home-canned food or a wound would raise botulism — both absent here. Certain drugs (e.g. aminoglycosides) unmask or worsen MG. The autoimmune family history fits the MG illness script.

history.find: She is frightened she is having a stroke like her father did, and is worried the double vision means she is going blind.
history.exp: Eliciting her specific fear (stroke, blindness) lets you target reassurance and explanation once the diagnosis is clear, and signals which differentials she most needs addressed.

pe.find: At rest there is mild right ptosis. On sustained upgaze for 45–60 seconds the right (then left) lid droops progressively. A brief Cogan's lid twitch is seen — the lid over-elevates then settles when she looks back to primary gaze.
pe.exp: Demonstrable fatigue of the levator on sustained upgaze, and Cogan's lid twitch, are bedside hallmarks of MG. Reproducing fatigability turns a symptom into a sign.
pe.lookingFor: Progressive lid drop on sustained upgaze; Cogan's twitch — demonstrable fatigability of ocular muscles.

pe.find: Complex, variable limitation of eye movements that does not respect a single cranial-nerve territory; diplopia worsens after sustained gaze in any direction.
pe.exp: MG can mimic any pattern of ophthalmoplegia, but the variability and lack of a single-nerve pattern are the clue — unlike a discrete third-nerve palsy. A pattern that is fixed and confined to one nerve should prompt a search for a compressive cause.
pe.lookingFor: Pattern not confined to one cranial nerve; fatigable, variable diplopia.

pe.find: Pupils are equal, round and briskly reactive to light. No anisocoria.
pe.exp: MG never affects the pupil. Normal pupils help exclude a pupil-involving third-nerve palsy (a posterior communicating artery aneurysm is the feared cause) and argue against botulism, which classically causes dilated, poorly reactive pupils.
pe.lookingFor: Pupil sparing — distinguishes MG from compressive 3rd-nerve palsy and from botulism.

pe.find: After a cold pack is held over the closed ptotic eye for two minutes, the ptosis improves by more than 2 mm.
pe.exp: Cooling slows acetylcholinesterase activity and improves neuromuscular transmission, lifting myasthenic ptosis. A >2 mm improvement is a simple bedside test with roughly 80% sensitivity and specificity for ocular MG.
pe.lookingFor: >2 mm lift in ptosis after cooling — supports a neuromuscular junction cause.

pe.find: Mild fatigable proximal weakness in the arms. Deep tendon reflexes are present and normal. Sensation is entirely intact.
pe.exp: Preserved reflexes and normal sensation are pivotal negatives: Guillain–Barré produces areflexia, and LEMS produces depressed reflexes that briefly potentiate after exercise. Normal sensation throughout argues against a peripheral neuropathy.
pe.lookingFor: Preserved reflexes + intact sensation — separates MG from GBS and peripheral neuropathy.

pe.find: Counting out loud on a single breath she reaches about 28 (normal >40). She is not in respiratory distress and speaks in full sentences.
pe.exp: The single-breath count is a quick surrogate for vital capacity (roughly count × 100 mL). A reduced count flags early respiratory muscle involvement and should trigger formal, serial FVC measurement — the airway is screened before, not after, things deteriorate.
pe.lookingFor: Single-breath count <40 — surrogate for falling vital capacity; triggers formal FVC.

pe.find: Afebrile, normotensive, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, regular pulse. No goitre, no proptosis.
pe.exp: A normal afebrile baseline argues against an infective or dysautonomic process and records the starting point against which serial respiratory observations are judged.

basic.find: FVC 28 mL/kg (normal >60); negative inspiratory force (NIF) −45 cmH2O. Above the thresholds that mandate ICU but reduced — to be repeated serially.
basic.exp: Formal respiratory measurement applies the '20/30/40' rule: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF less negative than −30 cmH2O, or MEP <40 cmH2O indicates a myasthenic crisis warranting ICU-level care (Claytor et al., Muscle & Nerve 2023). FVC is more reliable than NIF/MEP, which are effort-dependent. Serial trend matters more than a single value, and SpO2 falls late.

basic.find: TSH and free T4 within normal limits — no biochemical thyrotoxicosis.
basic.exp: Normal thyroid function makes thyroid eye disease/Graves an unlikely explanation for the ocular signs, and documents baseline thyroid status given the frequent co-occurrence of autoimmune thyroid disease with MG.

basic.find: No widened mediastinum or obvious anterior mediastinal mass on the plain film.
basic.exp: A CXR is a reasonable first look but is insensitive for thymoma — a normal film does not exclude it, so CT of the thorax is required once MG is suspected.

basic.find: Full blood count and renal panel (including potassium) all normal.
basic.exp: Baseline bloods exclude readily treatable mimics of weakness such as electrolyte disturbance (e.g. hypokalaemia) and provide a pre-treatment baseline.

advanced.find: Anti-AChR antibodies POSITIVE at an elevated titre — confirms autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
advanced.exp: Anti-AChR antibodies are diagnostic: sensitivity ~80–85% in generalised MG but under 50% in purely ocular disease, with specificity >98% (prospective multicentre data, 2024). A positive result in this clinical context confirms the diagnosis.

advanced.find: Not required once AChR is positive. Would be the next test if AChR were negative — positive in roughly 40% of AChR-negative generalised MG.
advanced.exp: Anti-MuSK antibodies define a distinct MG subtype (more bulbar/respiratory, often poorer response to anticholinesterases) and are tested when AChR antibodies are negative but MG is still suspected.

advanced.find: Low-frequency (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation shows a >10% decremental response in a proximal muscle — consistent with a postsynaptic NMJ disorder.
advanced.exp: A decrement of ≥10% is the accepted pathological threshold and confirms impaired neuromuscular transmission. If RNS is normal but suspicion remains, single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test (~95–99%). In LEMS and botulism the pattern differs — high-frequency stimulation shows an INCREMENT (facilitation).

advanced.find: Anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass approximately 3 cm — consistent with a thymoma.
advanced.exp: About 10–15% of MG patients have a thymoma, and thymic hyperplasia is commoner still. Every patient with newly diagnosed MG should have cross-sectional chest imaging, because identifying a thymoma changes downstream management.

advanced.find: Normal brainstem and cranial nerves; no infarct or demyelinating lesion.
advanced.exp: Reasonable when there is genuine doubt about a brainstem cause of the ophthalmoplegia. A normal study here helps exclude a brainstem stroke or demyelination, but the fluctuating, fatigable, pupil-sparing picture already pointed away from a fixed structural lesion.

advanced.find: Cerebrospinal fluid normal — normal protein and cell count. No useful diagnostic information for this presentation.
advanced.exp: An LP looking for albuminocytological dissociation belongs to the Guillain–Barré work-up, not MG. Ordering it here reflects anchoring on the wrong differential and exposes the patient to an unnecessary invasive test.

sigNegs.label: Pupils normal and reactive → not a pupil-involving 3rd-nerve palsy, and argues against botulism
Preserved reflexes + intact sensation → not Guillain–Barré and not LEMS
Weakness worsens with use (no post-exercise facilitation), no autonomic features → LEMS unlikely
Normal thyroid function → thyroid eye disease/Graves unlikely

findings.text: No orthopnoea and no breathlessness at rest — she lies flat and sleeps through the night
Single-breath count ~28 and speaking in full sentences, not in respiratory distress
FVC 28 mL/kg and NIF −45 cmH2O — above the 20/30/40 ICU thresholds, but reduced and to be monitored serially
Gradual, fluctuating onset over 3 weeks — brainstem stroke is sudden and maximal at onset
Variable, fatigable ophthalmoplegia not confined to one vascular territory, with normal pupils
MRI brain/brainstem normal — no infarct
No preceding diarrhoeal or respiratory illness; weakness fatigues with use rather than ascending steadily
Deep tendon reflexes preserved — Guillain–Barré (including Miller-Fisher) is characteristically areflexic
RNS shows a decrement typical of an NMJ disorder; nerve conduction studies would be needed to show the demyelination of GBS
No home-canned/fermented food and no wound; symptoms fluctuate rather than show a relentless descending paralysis
Pupils normal and reactive (botulism causes dilated, poorly reactive pupils); no dry mouth or other cholinergic-blockade features
High-frequency RNS would show an incremental (facilitating) response in botulism, opposite to the decrement seen here

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: Gradual fluctuating course over weeks — not the sudden onset of a brainstem stroke
Normal reactive pupils and no autonomic features — botulism much less likely
Reflexes preserved — argues strongly against GBS/Miller-Fisher
FVC/NIF above ICU thresholds — not in crisis now, continue serial monitoring

keyTeachingPoints: Fatigability is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis: weakness that worsens with sustained use and through the day, and recovers with rest. A clear diurnal pattern (better on waking, worse by evening) is the cheapest pointer to a neuromuscular junction disorder.

Assess respiratory function early and serially. Apply the 20/30/40 rule — FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF less negative than −30 cmH2O, or MEP <40 cmH2O indicates myasthenic crisis and ICU-level care (Claytor, Muscle & Nerve 2023). Oxygen desaturation is a late sign; the single-breath count is a useful bedside surrogate.

Anti-AChR antibodies confirm the diagnosis — sensitivity ~80–85% in generalised MG but <50% in purely ocular disease, specificity >98% (multicentre data, 2024). If AChR is negative, test anti-MuSK (positive in ~40% of AChR-negative cases).
Electrophysiology supports the diagnosis: a decrement ≥10% on low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation is pathological, and single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test (~95–99%) when RNS is normal.
Always image the chest (CT thorax) once MG is diagnosed: 10–15% of patients have a thymoma. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude it.

Normal pupils separate MG ophthalmoplegia from a pupil-involving third-nerve palsy (a posterior communicating artery aneurysm is the feared cause) and from botulism, which causes dilated, poorly reactive pupils.

Preserved reflexes and intact sensation separate MG from Guillain–Barré (areflexia) and from Lambert-Eaton syndrome — LEMS improves transiently with exercise, has autonomic features, and is linked to small-cell lung cancer.
The ice-pack test (>2 mm improvement in ptosis after cooling) is a simple, ~80% sensitive/specific bedside test that supports an NMJ cause.
cases.approachTitle: An Approach to Ptosis & Fatigable Weakness
cases.approachSub: Localise the lesion, prove the weakness is fatigable, then screen the airway
cases.approachText: Ptosis and diplopia can arise anywhere from muscle to brainstem. The discriminating question is whether the weakness is fatigable (worse with use, better with rest) and whether the pupil and reflexes are spared — features that localise to the neuromuscular junction and, specifically, to myasthenia gravis.

approachCats.name: Functional
approachCats.eg: Functional neurological disorder — positive signs, inconsistency

cases.approachInsight: The trap in this presentation is to localise too soon. A drooping lid and double vision instinctively suggest a third-nerve palsy or a stroke, and both are dangerous — but the moment the history reveals that the deficit fluctuates and fatigues, the lesion is pulled down to the neuromuscular junction. Two bedside negatives then do most of the discriminating work: a spared pupil takes a compressive third-nerve palsy and botulism off the table, and preserved reflexes separate MG from Guillain–Barré and Lambert-Eaton. What must never be deferred is the airway: fatigable bulbar and respiratory muscles are the reason MG is a must-not-miss, so vital capacity is measured early and tracked, long before any antibody result returns.
cases.expertNarrative: An experienced clinician hearing 'droopy lid and double vision, worse in the evening' is already thinking neuromuscular junction before the patient finishes the sentence — the diurnal, fatigable quality is that specific. The examination is then used to confirm fatigability (sustained upgaze, Cogan's twitch, the ice-pack test) and to harvest the negatives that exclude the dangerous mimics: a normal pupil, preserved reflexes, intact sensation. Crucially, the airway is assessed in the same breath as the eyes — a single-breath count and a formal FVC — because the patient who looks comfortable can still be sliding towards a crisis, and SpO2 will not warn you until it is late. Only then does the work-up move to the confirmatory layer: anti-AChR antibodies (anti-MuSK if negative), repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG, and CT of the thorax to look for a thymoma. The discipline is to hold stroke, Guillain–Barré and botulism live until a specific finding retires each, rather than collapsing onto MG because it is the expected answer.
cases.sensitivityNote: Anti-AChR antibodies are ~80–85% sensitive in generalised MG but under 50% in purely ocular MG, so a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis — anti-MuSK antibodies and single-fibre EMG (the most sensitive test, ~95–99%) extend the work-up. Bedside FVC is the most sensitive practical marker of early respiratory compromise and is far more reliable than waiting for oxygen desaturation.
cases.specificityNote: Fatigable ptosis with a spared pupil and preserved reflexes is highly specific for a neuromuscular junction disorder, and a positive anti-AChR antibody (specificity >98%) effectively seals MG. A >10% decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation is specific for impaired neuromuscular transmission, while an incremental (facilitating) response instead points to Lambert-Eaton syndrome or botulism.

cases.title: Right Upper Quadrant Pain & Fever
cases.secondaryApproach: An Approach to Right Upper Quadrant Pain
cases.patient: Mdm Liew Geok Choo, 50F, Business Executive
background: Recurrent biliary colic (≥5 episodes over 2 years)

validation.notes: Awaiting surgical sign-off on the imaging sequence (US first-line; ERCP reserved for proven ductal obstruction).

reasoning.bi05: Lipase is checked early specifically to exclude gallstone pancreatitis — a normal lipase keeps this in the cholecystitis lane.
reasoning.ai01: Ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory test (wall thickening, stones, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's) and also reads the CBD calibre.
reasoning.ai04: ERCP is NOT a diagnostic step here — with no jaundice, normal bilirubin and a non-dilated duct there is nothing to intervene on, and it risks iatrogenic pancreatitis.
reasoning.acute_calculous_cholecystitis: Positive Murphy's + systemic inflammation + characteristic ultrasound = Tokyo Guidelines 2018 definite acute cholecystitis.

cases.vignette: Mdm Liew Geok Choo is a 50-year-old business executive who presents with three days of constant pain in the right upper part of her abdomen, gradually worsening. She feels warm and has vomited twice, but has otherwise been coping at home until today.

history.lbl: Pain — site, onset, character, radiation, timing
history.find: Pain is in the right upper abdomen (right hypochondrium), came on over a few hours three days ago and has been constant and gradually worsening since. It does NOT radiate to the back or to the shoulder tip, and is NOT relieved by sitting forward. It is worse on movement and on taking a deep breath.
history.exp: A constant right-hypochondrial pain lasting well over 6 hours and worsening on inspiration points to the gallbladder. Radiation through to the back would raise pancreatitis; radiation to the shoulder tip would suggest diaphragmatic irritation. The duration (>6h) is what separates this from self-limiting biliary colic.

history.find: She has felt feverish (measured 37.8°C at home) but has had NO shaking chills or rigors.
history.exp: Low-grade fever fits acute cholecystitis. High swinging fevers with rigors would raise ascending cholangitis or an abscess — their absence is reassuring against a suppurative biliary infection.

history.find: No yellowing of the eyes or skin, no tea-coloured (dark) urine and no pale stools.
history.exp: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stools signals obstruction of the common bile duct (a stone in the duct, or cholangitis). Its absence here argues strongly against ascending cholangitis — there is no Charcot's triad.

history.lbl: Relation to fatty meals & previous similar episodes
history.find: Over the last two years she has had at least five episodes of right-upper pain coming on after fatty meals, each building over 3–4 hours then settling. Those were milder and she was never febrile. This episode is different: it has not settled and she now has a fever.
history.exp: A background of self-limiting post-fatty-meal pain is classic biliary colic. The change to persistent pain plus fever marks the transition to acute cholecystitis — a stone has impacted in the cystic duct, producing inflammation and infection.

history.find: Two episodes of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting. No haematemesis, no coffee-ground vomitus, no black stools and no rectal bleeding.
history.exp: Vomiting is common in biliary disease. Screening for haematemesis/melena keeps peptic ulcer disease and an upper GI bleed in view — both absent here.

history.find: She ate raw oysters at a function last week and has not been vaccinated against hepatitis A or B. No intravenous drug use, in a stable monogamous relationship, and has never received blood products.
history.exp: Recent raw shellfish in an unvaccinated person genuinely raises hepatitis A — useful 'noise' that must be weighed. It is later argued down by the liver panel, which shows neither a hepatocellular nor a cholestatic pattern.

history.find: No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no sweating and no palpitations.
history.exp: An inferior myocardial infarction can present as epigastric/right-upper pain. Screening for cardiac features (and doing an ECG and troponin) is mandatory before settling on a biliary cause.

history.find: No recent travel. She lives in an area with a current dengue cluster but has no rash, no severe muscle/joint or retro-orbital pain and no bleeding tendency.
history.exp: Dengue is endemic in Singapore and belongs on the differential for any fever. The absence of dengue-specific features, and a later negative NS1, set it aside.

history.lbl: Past medical, drugs, allergies, risk factors
history.find: Diabetes, hypertension and high cholesterol, all well controlled. No regular NSAIDs or steroids, no drug allergies (NKDA), no mechanical heart valve and no family history of jaundice or haemolytic anaemia.
history.exp: NSAIDs/steroids would raise peptic ulcer disease; a mechanical valve or haemolytic anaemia would raise pigment stones. The classic 'fat, female, forty, fertile' risk profile for cholesterol gallstones fits.

pe.find: Alert and reasonably comfortable. Mildly febrile at 37.8°C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 128/78. No scleral icterus and no pallor.
pe.exp: No clinical jaundice argues against biliary obstruction/cholangitis, and she is haemodynamically stable (not in septic shock). Fever plus tachycardia are the systemic component of the Tokyo criteria.
pe.lookingFor: Jaundice (cholangitis/CBD obstruction); haemodynamic instability (sepsis); pallor (bleeding).

pe.find: Tenderness with guarding over the right hypochondrium and epigastrium. Murphy's sign is POSITIVE (catching of the breath on deep RUQ palpation). The rest of the abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly and no palpable mass.
pe.exp: A positive Murphy's sign is the cardinal local sign of acute cholecystitis (Tokyo Guidelines 2018, Part A). Localised — rather than generalised — tenderness argues against a perforated viscus.
pe.lookingFor: Positive Murphy's sign (local TG18 criterion); a palpable tender mass (TG18 Grade II); generalised peritonism (perforation).

pe.find: No generalised rigidity and no rebound tenderness away from the right hypochondrium. Bowel sounds are present and normal.
pe.exp: Board-like rigidity, generalised rebound and absent bowel sounds would indicate a perforated viscus with peritonitis. Their absence keeps this a localised gallbladder process.

pe.find: Chest clear with equal air entry. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Pulse regular at 96.
pe.exp: A right basal pneumonia can refer pain to the right upper quadrant; a clear chest makes it less likely. Cardiac auscultation complements the ECG/troponin in screening for an ischaemic cause.

pe.find: No palpable gallbladder mass.
pe.exp: A palpable tender RUQ mass would upgrade severity (TG18 Grade II). A palpable NON-tender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier's sign) would instead point to malignant biliary obstruction — not the picture here.

pe.find: Mildly dry mucous membranes after vomiting. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable with no melena.
pe.exp: Assessing fluid status guides resuscitation; completing the examination with a DRE checks for occult GI bleeding.

basic.find: White cell count raised at 14.5 ×10⁹/L with neutrophilia. Haemoglobin and platelets normal.
basic.exp: Leukocytosis is the systemic-inflammation limb of the Tokyo criteria. A white cell count >18 ×10⁹/L would push severity towards TG18 Grade II.

basic.find: Mildly raised ALP and GGT. Bilirubin normal. ALT and AST normal — neither a cholestatic nor a hepatocellular pattern.
basic.exp: A markedly cholestatic panel (high bilirubin/ALP) would point to a CBD stone or cholangitis; a hepatocellular panel (high ALT/AST) to hepatitis. A normal bilirubin with only mildly raised ALP fits uncomplicated cholecystitis and argues against duct obstruction.

basic.find: CRP raised at 85 mg/L.
basic.exp: A raised CRP is part of the systemic-inflammation criterion in TG18 and provides a baseline to trend the response to treatment.

basic.find: Urea mildly raised with a small rise in creatinine — a pre-renal picture from vomiting and reduced intake.
basic.exp: Documents a pre-renal acute kidney injury and guides fluid resuscitation.

basic.find: Serum lipase 60 U/L (normal <140) — NOT elevated.
basic.exp: Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis, so lipase must be checked. A lipase >3× the upper limit of normal would reclassify this as acute pancreatitis (Revised Atlanta). A normal lipase keeps the diagnosis as cholecystitis.

basic.find: ECG shows sinus rhythm with no ischaemic changes. High-sensitivity troponin T normal.
basic.exp: Excludes an inferior myocardial infarction presenting as upper-abdominal pain.

basic.find: No free air under the diaphragm. No basal consolidation.
basic.exp: An erect chest film screens for pneumoperitoneum (a perforated viscus) and for a right basal pneumonia mimicking biliary pain.

basic.find: Dengue NS1 antigen negative.
basic.exp: In an endemic setting with a local cluster, a negative dengue test removes an important fever differential.

advanced.find: Thickened gallbladder wall (5 mm) with multiple intraluminal gallstones casting posterior acoustic shadows. Pericholecystic fluid present. Sonographic Murphy's sign positive. Common bile duct NOT dilated (normal calibre), with no ductal stone seen.
advanced.exp: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test and supplies the Tokyo 2018 imaging criterion: wall thickening, stones, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign confirm acute cholecystitis. A non-dilated CBD with no ductal stone argues against choledocholithiasis and cholangitis.

advanced.find: Gallbladder wall thickening, gallstones and pericholecystic fat stranding. No free air, no abscess or collection.
advanced.exp: CT is a useful second-line test when ultrasound is equivocal or unavailable overnight, and to look for complications (perforation, abscess, emphysematous cholecystitis). It is not preferred over ultrasound as the first test for uncomplicated cholecystitis.

advanced.find: Common bile duct of normal calibre with no filling defect — no choledocholithiasis.
advanced.exp: MRCP is the non-invasive way to interrogate the bile duct when there is concern about a CBD stone (deranged LFTs or a dilated duct). Here, with normal bilirubin and a non-dilated CBD, it is confirmatory-only and largely unnecessary — but it is the correct step BEFORE any thought of ERCP.

advanced.find: Not indicated. There is no jaundice, the bilirubin is normal and the duct is not dilated — there is no ductal obstruction to treat.
advanced.exp: ERCP is a therapeutic, invasive procedure reserved for proven CBD stones or cholangitis, and it carries a real risk of causing pancreatitis, bleeding or perforation. It is never a diagnostic test for cholecystitis. Reaching for ERCP here is the classic over-investigation error — image the duct non-invasively (MRCP/EUS) first if there is any concern.

sigNegs.label: No jaundice, dark urine or pale stools → ascending cholangitis / CBD obstruction unlikely (no Charcot's triad)
Normal serum lipase → acute pancreatitis excluded
Normal bilirubin, non-cholestatic / non-hepatocellular liver panel → choledocholithiasis and hepatitis less likely
No generalised peritonism, bowel sounds present → perforated viscus unlikely
Normal ECG and troponin → myocardial infarction less likely

findings.text: No jaundice, no dark urine and no rigors — Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) is incomplete
No scleral icterus; haemodynamically stable (no hypotension or confusion to suggest Reynolds' pentad)
Normal bilirubin, a non-dilated common bile duct on ultrasound and no ductal stone on MRCP
No chest pain, dyspnoea, diaphoresis or palpitations
ECG in sinus rhythm with no ischaemic changes and a normal high-sensitivity troponin
Pain does not radiate to the back and is not relieved by sitting forward
Serum lipase is normal (not >3× the upper limit of normal), so the Revised Atlanta biochemical criterion is not met
No sudden, severe, generalised abdominal pain
Localised RUQ tenderness only, no generalised peritonism, bowel sounds present
No free air under the diaphragm on the erect chest film or CT

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: Localised tenderness with no peritonism and present bowel sounds — perforation much less likely
Normal lipase — does not meet the Revised Atlanta biochemical threshold
Normal ECG and troponin — ischaemic cause excluded
Normal bilirubin and non-cholestatic panel — no biochemical evidence of duct obstruction

keyTeachingPoints: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) define acute cholecystitis by three parts: A — local signs (Murphy's sign, RUQ pain/mass/tenderness); B — systemic signs (fever, raised CRP, raised white cell count); C — characteristic imaging. A definite diagnosis needs A + B + C; A + B alone is a suspected diagnosis.

Biliary colic is self-limiting (typically <6 hours) and follows fatty meals; when the pain becomes persistent (>6 hours) and is accompanied by fever and a raised white cell count, the stone has impacted the cystic duct and the picture is acute cholecystitis.

The dangerous escalation is ascending cholangitis — Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice), and Reynolds' pentad with added hypotension and confusion. Look for jaundice, a cholestatic liver panel and a dilated CBD; their absence keeps the diagnosis at cholecystitis.
Always check lipase: gallstones are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis, and a lipase >3× the upper limit of normal would reclassify the patient (Revised Atlanta classification, 2012).

Ultrasound is the first-line investigation — gallbladder wall thickening (>3–4 mm), gallstones with posterior acoustic shadowing, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign — and it reads the CBD calibre to screen for ductal stones.

ERCP is NOT a diagnostic test for cholecystitis. It is an invasive, therapeutic procedure for proven CBD stones or cholangitis and risks causing pancreatitis. If a ductal stone is suspected, screen non-invasively with MRCP or EUS first.

TG18 severity grading drives urgency: Grade II (moderate) if white cell count >18 ×10⁹/L, a palpable tender RUQ mass, symptoms >72 hours, or marked local inflammation (gangrenous/emphysematous cholecystitis, abscess); Grade III (severe) if there is organ dysfunction.

Definitive treatment is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally early (within 72 hours). Watch for failure of conservative management (rising fever, worsening pain, peritonism) signalling empyema, gangrene or perforation; other complications include cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus, and (long term) gallbladder cancer.
cases.approachTitle: An Approach to Right Upper Quadrant Pain
cases.approachSub: Separate the biliary tree from the liver, pancreas, gut, heart and chest
cases.approachText: Right-upper-quadrant pain with fever is biliary until proven otherwise, but the job is to place it precisely: is this the gallbladder (cholecystitis), the duct (stone/cholangitis), the liver (hepatitis), the pancreas, or a referred cardiac/pleural cause? The discriminators are jaundice, the liver panel pattern, the lipase and the ultrasound.

approachCats.name: Referred — cardiac / pleural / tropical
approachCats.eg: Inferior MI, right basal pneumonia, dengue

cases.approachInsight: The trap in right-upper-quadrant pain is to stop at 'gallstones' and miss either the dangerous duct (cholangitis) or a referred killer (inferior MI). The clean way through is to ask three questions in order: is the duct obstructed (jaundice, dark urine, cholestatic panel, dilated CBD)? — if not, cholangitis and a retained stone fall away. Is the pancreas involved (back radiation, lipase >3× ULN)? — if not, pancreatitis falls away. Is this referred from the chest (ECG, troponin, chest film)? — if not, the heart and lung fall away. What remains, anchored by a positive Murphy's sign and a confirmatory ultrasound, is acute cholecystitis. Crucially, the absence of duct obstruction is also what tells you ERCP has no role — there is nothing to clear.
cases.expertNarrative: The experienced surgeon hears 'days of constant RUQ pain with fever on a background of fatty-food colic' and is already on cholecystitis, but spends the consultation deliberately excluding the things that change management. Jaundice and a cholestatic panel are hunted because cholangitis is the emergency that needs the duct cleared; a lipase is sent because gallstone pancreatitis sits one stone away; an ECG and troponin are done because an inferior MI hides in this exact location. The ultrasound is then used to confirm the gallbladder and — just as importantly — to read the bile duct. With a normal bilirubin, a non-dilated duct and no ductal stone, the reasoning closes: this is acute cholecystitis, and there is nothing for an ERCP to do. The discipline is to let the cheap, fast tests (lipase, LFT, ECG, ultrasound) retire each dangerous mimic rather than jumping to invasive imaging.
cases.sensitivityNote: Ultrasound is highly sensitive for gallstones and, combined with wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign, is sensitive for acute cholecystitis; a normal study in a convincing clinical picture should still prompt further imaging (CT or HIDA). Bedside Murphy's sign is sensitive but less specific. A normal bilirubin and non-dilated CBD are reassuring but do not completely exclude a small or passed ductal stone — which is why MRCP/EUS exist for the equivocal case.
cases.specificityNote: A positive sonographic Murphy's sign with gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid is highly specific for acute cholecystitis. Charcot's triad is specific for cholangitis but insensitive (present in a minority); its absence does not fully exclude the diagnosis, so the liver panel and duct calibre are checked. A lipase >3× the upper limit of normal is specific for pancreatitis and would change the diagnosis entirely.

cases.title: Epigastric Pain Radiating to the Back
background: Gallstones noted on a previous ultrasound

validation.notes: Awaiting GI/HPB sign-off on the investigation order (diagnosis = pain + lipase; ducts assessed by MRCP/EUS before ERCP; CT deferred for necrosis).

reasoning.bi05: Lipase is the pivotal test — a level >3× the upper limit of normal with characteristic pain already satisfies the Revised Atlanta diagnosis, BEFORE any cross-sectional imaging.
reasoning.ai01: Ultrasound is first-line to establish the gallstone aetiology and read the CBD — not to 'diagnose' the pancreatitis, which is already established.
reasoning.ai03: With a suspected but unproven duct stone and NO cholangitis, MRCP (or EUS) is the correct next step to image the duct non-invasively.
reasoning.ai05: ERCP is withheld: there is no cholangitis and no confirmed ongoing obstruction, so a diagnostic/early ERCP only adds the risk of worsening the pancreatitis.
reasoning.ai02: Acutely, CT adds little to a typical diagnosis and underestimates necrosis early — it is most useful deferred to ~72–96 h if the patient deteriorates.
reasoning.acute_pancreatitis: Characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back + lipase >3× ULN meets 2 of 3 Revised Atlanta criteria; gallstones supply the aetiology.

cases.vignette: Mdm Goh Swee Lan is a 52-year-old hawker who presents with two days of severe, constant pain in the upper-middle of her abdomen. It came on suddenly and has not let up. She has vomited twice and feels feverish.

history.lbl: Pain — site, onset, character, radiation, relief
history.find: Severe, constant, boring epigastric pain that began suddenly two days ago and has not eased. It radiates straight THROUGH to the back, is slightly better sitting up and leaning forward, and worse lying flat.
history.exp: Epigastric pain boring through to the back, eased by leaning forward, is the classic pancreatitis script. But back radiation also overlaps with an aortic catastrophe, and epigastric pain with peptic ulcer disease — so the history must actively separate these.

history.lbl: Cardiac & aortic screen — chest pain, tearing, migration
history.find: The pain did NOT start in the chest and migrate, and is not 'tearing' or 'ripping'. No crushing chest pain, breathlessness, sweating or palpitations. No blackouts, limb weakness or facial droop.
history.exp: A sudden tearing chest pain migrating to the back is aortic dissection; crushing chest pain with diaphoresis is myocardial infarction. Both are can't-miss causes of epigastric/back pain and must be screened before anchoring on pancreatitis.

history.find: No yellowing of eyes or skin, no dark urine or pale stools, and no shaking rigors. Fever is low-grade (37.9°C) without chills.
history.exp: Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) signals ascending cholangitis — the finding that, if present, would justify urgent ERCP. Its absence here is central to the investigation strategy: there is no cholangitis to drain.

history.lbl: Vomiting and GI bleeding / ulcer risk
history.find: Nausea with two episodes of non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting. No haematemesis or melena. No long-term NSAID or steroid use and no known peptic ulcer or H. pylori.
history.exp: A perforated or bleeding peptic ulcer is a key epigastric differential; the absence of bleeding and ulcer risk factors makes it less likely but does not exclude perforation, which the examination and erect film address.

history.lbl: Aetiology screen — gallstones, alcohol, lipids, drugs, metabolic
history.find: Known gallstones on a previous ultrasound and longstanding post-meal dyspepsia. Only occasional, small amounts of alcohol. Hyperlipidaemic with a history of high triglycerides. No recent ERCP or OGD, no offending drugs, no symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and no recent mumps.
history.exp: Walking through the 'I GET SMASHED' aetiologies, the leading candidates here are gallstones and hypertriglyceridaemia. Establishing the cause matters because gallstone disease is the part that may eventually need duct clearance and cholecystectomy.

history.find: No bloody diarrhoea and the pain is not strikingly out of proportion to the examination. No atrial fibrillation or known vascular disease.
history.exp: Mesenteric ischaemia classically gives pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen, often in a vasculopath or someone with AF — a quick screen keeps this dangerous mimic in view.

history.find: Lives in an area with a current dengue cluster, but has no rash, severe myalgia, retro-orbital pain or bleeding tendency.
history.exp: Dengue is endemic and can cause abdominal pain and deranged bloods; the absence of dengue features and a later negative test set it aside.

history.find: Diabetes, hypertension and high cholesterol, reasonably controlled (HbA1c 6.0%). Works as a hawker with a rich, fatty diet. No previous surgery, NKDA.
history.exp: The metabolic background (diabetes, hyperlipidaemia) and diet reinforce the gallstone/triglyceride aetiology and matter for risk and recurrence.

pe.find: Looks unwell and prefers to sit forward. Heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, temperature 37.9°C, blood pressure 114/72, oxygen saturation 95% on room air — meeting SIRS criteria.
pe.exp: Tachycardia, tachypnoea and fever indicate a systemic inflammatory response. Tachypnoea and a borderline saturation are early warnings of severe disease (third-spacing, effusion, evolving ARDS) and feed the severity score.
pe.lookingFor: SIRS (HR, RR, temp, WCC); early respiratory compromise (RR, SpO₂) signalling severe pancreatitis.

pe.find: Epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, but NO generalised peritonism. Murphy's sign negative. No pulsatile expansile mass and no organomegaly. Bowel sounds present but reduced.
pe.exp: Epigastric tenderness with a soft remainder fits pancreatitis. A negative Murphy's sign points away from cholecystitis; the absence of a pulsatile expansile mass is reassuring (though not definitive) against an abdominal aortic aneurysm; reduced bowel sounds suggest an ileus.
pe.lookingFor: Murphy's negative (vs cholecystitis); no pulsatile mass (vs AAA); peritonism (vs perforation); ileus.

pe.find: No board-like rigidity and no generalised rebound. Bowel sounds, though reduced, are present.
pe.exp: Generalised peritonitis with a silent, rigid abdomen would indicate a perforated viscus. The localised epigastric signs here argue against free perforation.

pe.find: No flank (Grey-Turner) or periumbilical (Cullen) bruising.
pe.exp: These are late, infrequent signs of severe haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Their absence is expected early and does not exclude severe disease.

pe.lbl: Cardiovascular — pulses, BP both arms, murmurs
pe.find: Blood pressure equal in both arms, no radio-femoral delay, no early diastolic (aortic regurgitation) murmur, peripheral pulses all present.
pe.exp: These findings are reassuring against an aortic dissection — but note that equal arm pressures and present pulses do NOT exclude dissection, so a high clinical suspicion still warrants CT aortography.

pe.find: Mildly reduced air entry at both bases with oxygen saturation 95%.
pe.exp: Basal atelectasis and pleural effusions are common in pancreatitis, and hypoxia is part of both the severity score and the spectrum towards ARDS.

basic.find: White cell count raised at 17 ×10⁹/L. Haematocrit elevated (haemoconcentration). Platelets normal.
basic.exp: Leukocytosis is one of the modified Glasgow (Imrie) severity criteria (white cells >15 ×10⁹/L). A high haematocrit reflects third-space fluid loss and predicts a more severe course.

basic.find: Urea raised at 9 mmol/L with a rise in creatinine (acute kidney injury). Glucose 12 mmol/L. Bicarbonate and ketones do not suggest DKA.
basic.exp: Urea (>16 mmol/L) and glucose (>10 mmol/L) are Glasgow severity criteria; a pre-renal AKI reflects hypovolaemia and drives aggressive fluid resuscitation. Checking ketones/bicarbonate excludes DKA as a cause of the abdominal pain.

basic.find: Corrected calcium 2.0 mmol/L (low-normal/mildly low). Magnesium and phosphate normal.
basic.exp: Hypocalcaemia (<2 mmol/L) is a Glasgow criterion and a marker of severity (fat saponification). It is also worth noting hypercalcaemia can be a CAUSE of pancreatitis — so calcium cuts both ways.

basic.find: ALT mildly raised (a clue to gallstone aetiology). Bilirubin only marginally raised; not a frankly cholestatic picture. LDH and albumin recorded for the Glasgow score.
basic.exp: A raised ALT supports a gallstone cause. A markedly cholestatic panel with a high bilirubin would instead suggest a retained duct stone or cholangitis and push towards duct imaging. LDH (>600) and albumin (<32 g/L) are Glasgow severity markers.

basic.find: Serum lipase 850 U/L — more than three times the upper limit of normal (<140).
basic.exp: With characteristic pain, a lipase >3× the upper limit of normal already satisfies 2 of the 3 Revised Atlanta criteria — the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is made here, biochemically, WITHOUT needing a CT scan. Lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase.

basic.find: PaO₂ 9.5 kPa on room air with a mild metabolic acidosis and a modestly raised lactate.
basic.exp: PaO₂ (<8 kPa) is a Glasgow criterion; hypoxia and a rising lactate flag evolving organ dysfunction and the need for closer monitoring (HD/ICU).

basic.find: CRP 180 mg/L.
basic.exp: CRP is used to trend severity — a value >150 mg/L at 48 hours correlates with severe pancreatitis and the development of necrosis.

basic.find: ECG in sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes; troponin normal.
basic.exp: Excludes a myocardial infarction presenting as epigastric pain; sinus tachycardia simply reflects pain and the systemic inflammatory response.

basic.find: Clotting and group-and-match sent as a baseline (in case intervention is needed). Dengue NS1 negative.
basic.exp: Baseline coagulation and crossmatch are prudent before any possible endoscopic or surgical intervention; the negative dengue test removes an endemic differential.

advanced.find: Gallstones present within the gallbladder. Common bile duct of normal calibre with no definite ductal stone seen. The pancreas is poorly visualised due to overlying bowel gas.
advanced.exp: Ultrasound is first-line — not to 'diagnose' the pancreatitis (already established by pain + lipase) but to establish the gallstone aetiology and to read the bile duct. A non-dilated duct with no visible stone lowers the pre-test probability of a retained CBD stone.

advanced.find: Oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding; no necrosis and no free air. (Performed here largely to exclude other intra-abdominal pathology.)
advanced.exp: Acutely, CT is NOT required to diagnose pancreatitis when the history and lipase are typical, and it UNDERESTIMATES necrosis in the first 72 hours. Its real value is deferred — at ~72–96 hours or on deterioration — to assess for necrosis and complications. Early routine CT is low-yield (though often done in practice to exclude other diagnoses).

advanced.find: No retained common bile duct stone; duct calibre normal.
advanced.exp: When a CBD stone is suspected (gallstone aetiology, mildly deranged LFTs) but there is NO cholangitis, MRCP is the correct non-invasive way to image the duct — and it is done BEFORE any ERCP. Here it confirms there is no ductal stone to clear.

advanced.find: No microlithiasis or small ampullary/CBD stone identified.
advanced.exp: EUS is an alternative to MRCP for screening the duct before ERCP, and is especially sensitive for small stones and microlithiasis that MRCP can miss. Like MRCP, it precedes — and frequently spares — an ERCP.

advanced.find: Not indicated as a first step. There is no cholangitis and no confirmed or persistent ductal obstruction, so there is nothing to clear — and a diagnostic ERCP would only add the risk of worsening the pancreatitis.
advanced.exp: This is the central error this case tests. ERCP is therapeutic, reserved for gallstone pancreatitis WITH cholangitis or ongoing biliary obstruction (ACG 2024). Doing it early/diagnostically — before MRCP or EUS has even confirmed a duct stone — exposes the patient to post-ERCP pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation. The correct order is: diagnose with pain + lipase, find the aetiology on ultrasound, screen the duct with MRCP/EUS, and only then ERCP if a stone with obstruction/cholangitis is proven.

advanced.find: Aorta of normal calibre with no dissection flap and no aneurysm.
advanced.exp: Appropriate when the back-radiating pain raises genuine concern for aortic dissection or a leaking aneurysm — because clinical signs alone cannot exclude them. Normal here, retiring the aortic differential.

sigNegs.label: No tearing/migratory chest-to-back pain; no crushing chest pain → aortic dissection and MI less likely
No jaundice, dark urine or rigors → no Charcot's triad → ascending cholangitis less likely (and no indication for ERCP)
No generalised peritonism, bowel sounds present → perforated viscus less likely
Equal arm BPs, no radio-femoral delay, pulses intact → reassuring against dissection (not definitive)

findings.text: Pain did not begin in the chest and migrate, and is not tearing or ripping in quality
Equal blood pressures in both arms, no radio-femoral delay and no aortic regurgitation murmur — reassuring, though not by themselves definitive
CT aortogram shows a normal aorta with no dissection flap
No jaundice, dark urine or rigors — Charcot's triad is absent
Bilirubin only marginally raised, a non-dilated duct on ultrasound and no ductal stone on MRCP — no obstructed, infected duct
No crushing chest pain, dyspnoea or diaphoresis
ECG with no ischaemic changes and a normal troponin
Localised epigastric tenderness without generalised peritonism; bowel sounds present
No free air on the CT (or erect chest film)

mnmExpectedDemotion.note: Normal ECG and troponin — ischaemic cause excluded
Bilirubin only marginally raised, not a cholestatic obstructive picture
No peritonism and bowel sounds present — free perforation unlikely
CT aortogram normal — dissection excluded

keyTeachingPoints: The Revised Atlanta classification (2012) diagnoses acute pancreatitis when 2 of 3 are present: (1) characteristic abdominal pain, (2) lipase or amylase >3× the upper limit of normal, (3) cross-sectional imaging findings. With typical pain and a lipase >3× ULN, the diagnosis is made BEFORE — and without needing — a CT scan.

Investigation ORDER matters. Diagnose with pain + lipase; establish the gallstone aetiology and read the duct on ultrasound; if a CBD stone is suspected without cholangitis, screen the duct non-invasively with MRCP or EUS; reserve ERCP for proven obstruction or cholangitis.

ERCP is NOT a first-line or diagnostic test in acute pancreatitis. Early/diagnostic ERCP — especially before MRCP/EUS has confirmed a duct stone — risks worsening the pancreatitis and causing bleeding or perforation. It is indicated for gallstone pancreatitis WITH cholangitis or ongoing biliary obstruction (ACG 2024).

CT is not needed acutely for a typical diagnosis and underestimates necrosis in the first 72 hours; its value is in the deferred scan (~72–96 h or on deterioration) to assess necrosis and complications. In practice it is often done early to exclude other intra-abdominal pathology.

Stratify severity early. The modified Glasgow (Imrie) score (PANCREAS: PaO₂ <8 kPa, Age >55, Neutrophils/WCC >15, Calcium <2 mmol/L, Renal urea >16 mmol/L, Enzymes LDH >600, Albumin <32 g/L, Sugar/glucose >10 mmol/L) — a score ≥3 within 48 hours indicates severe disease and HD/ICU-level care.

Aortic dissection and an inferior MI both present with epigastric pain radiating to the back and must be screened (and imaged if suspected) — equal arm pressures and intact pulses are reassuring but do NOT exclude dissection.

Cornerstones of management are aggressive fluid resuscitation, analgesia, nil by mouth with early enteral nutrition as tolerated, and treating the cause. Gallstone pancreatitis is followed by same-admission cholecystectomy once the patient recovers, to prevent recurrence (≈ high recurrence within weeks if the gallbladder is left in).

Complications are local (pseudocyst, sterile or infected necrosis, pseudoaneurysm, exocrine/endocrine insufficiency) and systemic (ARDS, AKI, DIC, hypocalcaemia) — infected necrosis is suspected when a patient deteriorates ~1 week in with persisting fever and pain.
cases.approachSub: Place the pancreas among the vascular, cardiac, biliary and gut causes — then investigate in the right order
cases.approachText: Epigastric pain radiating to the back has a short list of causes that kill (aortic dissection, MI, perforation, mesenteric ischaemia) and a short list that are common (pancreatitis, peptic ulcer, biliary disease). Pancreatitis is diagnosed cheaply and early with pain + lipase; the harder skill is sequencing the imaging — duct before ERCP, CT deferred.

approachCats.name: Vascular
approachCats.eg: Aortic dissection, leaking AAA, mesenteric ischaemia

cases.approachInsight: There are two separate skills this case examines. The first is the differential of epigastric/back pain, where the discipline is to screen the vascular and cardiac killers (dissection, MI) and the biliary emergency (cholangitis) before settling on the common answer. The second — and the one most often done badly — is investigation order. Pancreatitis is a clinical–biochemical diagnosis: characteristic pain plus a lipase >3× ULN meets Revised Atlanta, so a CT is not needed to make the diagnosis and is actively misleading if used early to gauge necrosis. The aetiology and the duct are then assessed by ultrasound, and a suspected duct stone WITHOUT cholangitis is chased with MRCP or EUS — never a diagnostic ERCP, which can ignite the very pancreatitis you are treating. ERCP earns its place only when a stone is obstructing or cholangitis is present.
cases.expertNarrative: Confronted with two days of boring epigastric pain through to the back, the experienced clinician makes the diagnosis quickly and cheaply — send a lipase, and with a typical history a level over three times normal closes it under Revised Atlanta. The energy then goes two ways. First, to the killers that share this pain: a focused history and examination screen for dissection and MI, and if suspicion is real the aorta is imaged with CT — because, as the examination notes, equal arm pressures do not exclude a dissection. Second, to severity and aetiology: a Glasgow score is assembled from the bloods and gas, fluids are run hard, and an ultrasound finds the gallstones and reads the duct. The discriminating judgement is what NOT to do — not to order an early CT expecting it to grade necrosis, and above all not to send the patient for a diagnostic ERCP. With no cholangitis and an unobstructed duct, the duct is interrogated non-invasively by MRCP or EUS, and ERCP is held in reserve. The case rewards the student who diagnoses on lipase, stratifies on Glasgow, and sequences the imaging correctly.
cases.sensitivityNote: Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase and remains elevated longer, making it the test of choice; however the magnitude of elevation does not correlate with severity. CT is insensitive for necrosis in the first 72 hours, so an early normal-looking scan is falsely reassuring — severity is judged clinically and by score, not by early CT. MRCP and EUS are both sensitive for choledocholithiasis, with EUS superior for small stones and microlithiasis.
cases.specificityNote: A lipase >3× the upper limit of normal with characteristic pain is specific enough to diagnose acute pancreatitis without imaging. Charcot's triad is specific for cholangitis but insensitive — its absence does not fully exclude a duct stone, which is why the duct is imaged when LFTs are deranged. A normal CT aortogram is definitive for excluding dissection, which clinical signs cannot do.

cases.title: Hand Tremor at Rest
background: Not on any antipsychotics or anti-emetics

validation.notes: Awaiting neurology sign-off — PD is a clinical diagnosis; DaTscan/MRI used to separate mimics.

reasoning.h06: The drug history is checked early and deliberately — drug-induced parkinsonism is the reversible must-not-miss and is easy to overlook.
reasoning.ai01: DaTscan is the discriminator withheld to this stage: it separates degenerative parkinsonism (PD) from essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism (both have a normal scan).
reasoning.parkinson_s_disease: Asymmetrical rest tremor + bradykinesia + cogwheel rigidity, no Parkinson-plus red flags, abnormal DaTscan and good levodopa response = idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

cases.vignette: Mr Tan Ah Seng is a 68-year-old retiree brought in by his daughter because of a tremor in his right hand that she has noticed over the past several months. She says it is most obvious when his hand is resting in his lap.

history.lbl: Tremor — rest vs action, asymmetry, what changes it
history.find: The tremor is present at REST — most obvious when the hand lies still in his lap or while watching television — and it eases when he reaches for something. It is worse on the right than the left (asymmetrical) and has a 'pill-rolling' quality. It worsens with stress and disappears in sleep.
history.exp: A rest tremor that improves with voluntary movement and is asymmetrical is the signature of Parkinson's disease. An action/postural tremor that worsens on reaching (and improves with alcohol) would instead point to essential tremor — the single most useful distinction in tremor.

history.find: His handwriting has become noticeably smaller (micrographia) and he is slower doing up buttons and other fine tasks with the right hand.
history.exp: Bradykinesia — slowness with decrementing amplitude of repetitive movement — is the essential feature of parkinsonism in the MDS 2015 criteria; micrographia is a classic everyday manifestation.

history.find: He feels stiff, walks with smaller shuffling steps and reduced right arm swing, and stoops slightly. He has NOT had early falls.
history.exp: A shuffling gait with reduced arm swing fits PD. The absence of EARLY, prominent falls is important — early falls would point to progressive supranuclear palsy (a Parkinson-plus syndrome).

history.lbl: Non-motor features — smell, sleep, bowels, mood
history.find: His sense of smell has been reduced for over a year, he acts out his dreams at night (shouting, thrashing), and he is constipated.
history.exp: Hyposmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder and constipation are prodromal non-motor features that often predate the motor signs and strongly support a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease.

history.lbl: Red-flag screen for Parkinson-plus (cognition, autonomic, falls, gaze)
history.find: No early memory loss or hallucinations, no fainting or marked light-headedness on standing, no early falls, and no trouble looking up or down.
history.exp: Early dementia/hallucinations (Lewy body), early severe autonomic failure (MSA), early falls and vertical gaze problems (PSP) are red flags for a Parkinson-plus syndrome. Their absence favours idiopathic PD.

history.find: He takes only an ACE inhibitor and metformin. He is NOT on any antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or other dopamine-blocking drug.
history.exp: Drug-induced parkinsonism — from dopamine-blocking antipsychotics and anti-emetics — is REVERSIBLE and the key must-not-miss in any new parkinsonism. Reviewing the drug list is mandatory; a normal DaTscan would further confirm it if a culprit drug were present.

history.lbl: Alcohol response & family history of tremor
history.find: A drink of alcohol does NOT settle the tremor, and there is no strong family history of tremor.
history.exp: Essential tremor classically improves transiently with alcohol and runs in families (autosomal dominant). Neither is true here, arguing against essential tremor.

history.find: No liver disease or behavioural change, and no heat intolerance, palpitations or weight loss.
history.exp: Wilson's disease (copper accumulation) must be screened in YOUNGER patients with movement disorder; hyperthyroidism produces a fine action tremor. Both are screened biochemically.

pe.lbl: General inspection, facial expression & lying/standing BP
pe.find: Reduced facial expression (hypomimia) and soft speech (hypophonia). Lying and standing blood pressures show no significant postural drop.
pe.exp: Facial masking and hypophonia are typical of PD. A large postural blood-pressure drop would raise multiple system atrophy (a Parkinson-plus syndrome with early autonomic failure).
pe.lookingFor: Hypomimia/hypophonia (PD); significant postural BP drop (MSA).

pe.lbl: Cardinal motor signs — rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia
pe.find: Asymmetrical resting pill-rolling tremor (right > left). Cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist. Finger-tapping shows progressive slowing and decrementing amplitude (bradykinesia).
pe.exp: Bradykinesia plus rest tremor and rigidity establishes parkinsonism (MDS 2015). The marked asymmetry favours idiopathic Parkinson's disease over the more symmetrical Parkinson-plus and vascular forms.
pe.lookingFor: Bradykinesia + rest tremor + cogwheel rigidity (parkinsonism); asymmetry (favours PD).
